Our analysis is based on 312 thousand cosmic ray events detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, having energies above 4 EeV and an azimuthal angle between 15 degrees and 165 degrees from the Earth.  We identified the anisotropy in these events' arrival directions using a new approach that considers both the amplitude and the shape of the anisotropy.  We found a strong anisotropy with a dipole amplitude of (6.61 ± 0.60) x 10^-3 of the universe's surface area, exhibiting the same orientation previously reported.  Its fit shape indicates significant alignment with the Galactic center, and we observed an increase in anisotropy amplitude with energy, classified into two patterns for two energy ranges: below 7 EeV and between 7 EeV and 13 EeV.  We also detected anisotropy in the multiplicity of the closest neighbors to each detected cosmic ray, with an amplitude of (0.788 ± 0.083) for energies above 4 EeV.  This anisotropy's energy pattern differs from that of the cosmic ray distribution itself.  We interpreted these findings within the framework of extragalactic magnetic fields, considering both charged particles and their grandparents, with assumptions about their interactions and the distribution of cosmic sources.  Our analysis revealed that the anisotropy of the nearest neighbor distribution suggests larger magnetic field strengths than previously thought, while the energy patterns of both anisotropies pointed to the presence of higher-energy particles than expected, which were, however, blocked by magnetic fields before reaching Earth.  Therefore, we advocated for the need to re-examine the assumptions about the interactions of cosmic particles with magnetic fields and to consider new possibilities about the distribution of their sources.  Our study further highlighted the significance of investigating the anisotropy of cosmic rays with energies above 4 EeV using enhanced detectors and new approaches that consider both amplitude and shape.  Our primary findings have been validated through simulations of Auger with an expanded field of view, indicating that more precise measurements of anisotropy with higher statistics and larger acceptance would be feasible with upgraded detectors in the future.  Finally, we outlined strategies for future experiments, including the Auger Next Generation Telescope, to make more precise measurements of cosmic anisotropy across various energies and scenarios. Unlike traditional approach that relies on explicit programming, this method enables robots to excel at manipulation by learning from limited demonstrations. During demonstrations, operators provide feedback to learners about tasks' local success, guiding the learner's representation of action space through correlation-based learning. As a result, Neural descriptor fields yield robust representation capable of executing tasks successfully with mere access to the same action space. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by teaching a robot to sort objects of varying shape and size using minimal demonstrations. Our method surpasses standards for learning from demonstrations by reducing required demonstrations twenty-fold while maintaining the same success rate. Moreover, Neural descriptor fields exhibit a small and scalable architecture, suitable for real-world robot applications. With its versatility and action-space generalization, this method promises a wide range of successful manipulation tasks, beyond the ones presented in this research. Our results show that near the point of highest achievable TAP free energy, the algorithm's performance follows a power law with the same strength as the TAP free energy, but with the opposite sign. This strong connection between the two measures allows us to resolve the dynamics of the TAP free energy at the point of its maximum, which we find to be marked by a non-equilibrium phase transition with contrasting dynamics on either side. Accurate object pose estimation in complex and real-world scenes remains a challenging task, especially when there are many competing objects. 4D spatio-temporal point clouds have shown promise in modeling dynamic environments, but current techniques fail to account for an essential structural element - projection relationships.  We introduce a novel method called Projective Structure Network (PS-Net) that incorporates projection relationships to enable efficient pose estimation for single-frame and multi-frame point clouds.  Our approach represents scene structure as a directed graph, incorporating projection relationships between projection nodes and a pose node that drives feature extraction through a custom designed network.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of PS-Net by achieving the lowest pose estimation error on the SUN12B dataset and the largest CMU Panoptic dataset subset.  Further, our method is versatile and capable of estimating the pose of single-frame and multi-frame point clouds with the same network architecture.  We showcase the robustness of our method by conducting an experiment on the SUN12B dataset with an order of magnitude larger than the training set.  Our approach provides a solid foundation for further improvement of the pose estimation task in challenging scenes.  Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhongyury/PS-Net.  Our project page is available at: https://zhongyury.github.io/PS-Net/.  Our dataset extension rules are available at: https://cmupanoptic.org/dataset_extension_rules.html.  Our technique is a starting point for modeling projection relationships in object pose estimation tasks.  We suggest future directions such as incorporating our method with learning-based pose estimation networks and exploring its applications on other computer vision tasks.  Our technique is a potential solution for modeling complex scenes with dynamic objects.  We propose a framework for extending the current dataset guidelines with projection information, which could improve model generalizability on real-world scenes.  Our framework is versatile and can be adapted to other 3D and 4D point cloud datasets. This study investigates how the pressure within a cavity beneath an aircraft surface affects dynamics, specifically for surface seals near high-speed jets. Due to the limited availability of experimental data, research is primarily conducted using numerical modeling, utilizing an unstructured, high-reliability, and high-speed-compliant solver for fluid dynamics and a coupled solution strategy. A surface seal model with a circular shape is analyzed, with pressures inside the cavity ranging from negative to positive values and jet velocities from 450 to 900 meters per second. The results indicate that the pressure within the cavity plays a crucial role in surface seal dynamics, with increased pressure causing the seal to lift off the surface, especially at higher jet velocities. Furthermore, the research reveals that the pressure's influence dominates other surface seal dynamics factors, especially at high speeds, and that the surface seal's state can be either stuck to the surface or lifted off, depending on the pressure and jet velocity dynamics. Additionally, a surface seal state model is proposed and tested, with the results showing that this model effectively predicts surface seal states through a nonlinear switch between the stuck and lifted states. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates a surface seal state trend, with the state alternating between stuck and lifted states as the jet velocity increases. Ultimately, the research provides insights into surface seal dynamics, especially for aircraft equipped with retropackets or tailkits. Given the limited scope of this study, further research is necessary to explore other surface seal shapes and cave cavity configurations. The proposed model can be utilized in future studies to investigate aircraft state predictions and control through surface seal dynamics analysis. In particular, it has been shown that positive-norm state solutions can be obtained when the condensate exhibits positive norm characteristics. Furthermore, the effect leads to the creation of a polarized charge distribution with a specific intensity and polarization orientation. The generalized Witten effect also exhibits symmetry properties such as dipole-like behavior in scalar gauge fields and spin-like behavior in the case of spin gauge fields. Additionally, it has been discovered that the effect can result in the condensate returning to a state of zero charge, which can be described by either exponential or sinusoidal functions, depending on the specific gauge field. The effect's impact on both massless and massive gauge fields has been examined, including the emergence of a mass term in the case of massive gauge fields. The interaction between the condensate and the gauge field also gives rise to the creation of massive charged states from a vacuum state in quantum gravity. Theoretical analysis of this compound reveals a high degree of charge instability among its iron atoms, which is reflected in a unique electronic structure. As a result, strong covalency leads to an incorrect prediction of metal oxidation state through the LDA component, emphasizing the need for accurate analysis of the total density of states. Moreover, the absence of any antiferromagnetic interaction among the neighboring iron atoms can be explained by examining the specific arrangement of its electron density, which results from optimizing the on-site Coulomb interaction. Ultimately, our study of cubanite provides a comprehensive understanding of its intimate relationship between electronic structure, crystal symmetry, and magnetism. The theoretical framework used in this study has been applied to a broader class of compounds with nonmagnetic sublattices, revealing a universal tendency for ferromagnetic ordering. The question of why cubanite remains so rare on Earth, despite being a possible product of magmatic-hydrothermal activity, is an area that requires further investigation. However, the magnitude of these oscillations can be impacted by the strength of this coupling, especially when it's too strong, where multi-phonon modes become significant and the Rabi-like behavior loses definition. In the case study presented here, investigators successfully induced Rabi-like oscillations between the system's second- and first-order cavity modes rather than ground and excited states, demonstrating a novel cavity geometry's ability to extend the coupling strength range where Rabi-like behavior persists. By adjusting the frequency of the driving laser, researchers demonstrated a specific cavity geometry's ability to produce stable Rabi oscillations in the quantum dot even when the coupling is too strong, primarily due to the presence of blue detuning. Moreover, the research uncovered a cubic relationship between the squared amplitude of these Rabi oscillations and the difference between the laser frequency and the cavity mode frequency. Additionally, a theoretical model was developed in tandem with the experiment, offering valuable insights into the system's dynamics. Despite the limited investigation of higher-order cavity modes in quantum dot-acoustic cavity systems, this research opens the door for exploring such modes and their potential benefits, including those related to non-classical light generation. The study's findings also have implications for developing reliable methods for detecting cavity modes in systems with lossy superconducting mirrors. The novel cavity design utilized in this research demonstration allows for larger coupling strengths and higher frequency cavity modes, presenting a promising configuration for implementing cavity quantum electrodynamics in solid-state systems. The role of the laser's phase noise in these systems has not been thoroughly explored, as seen in this research where a positive laser detuning was found to lead to the quantum dot's stable entanglement with the acoustic cavity rather than its decay. The investigation revealed that the conditions for achieving stable Rabi oscillations in quantum dot-acoustic cavity systems are more stringent than those required for single-photon entanglement. However, finding such stable Rabi oscillations in these systems can lead to a significant increase in the magnitude of the generated entanglement. Although this research was conducted using a specific quantum dot, the findings suggest that single-dot systems can serve as robust, stable Rabi oscillators for a wide range of coupling strengths. The study's results are expected to contribute to the development of solid-state cavity quantum electrodynamics systems capable of generating non-classical light over extended periods. Recent studies on herringbone lattices, which consist of coupled oscillators in specific patterns, have revealed exotic phenomena such as universal robustness and precise lattice synchronization. However, the narrow range of frequency ratios applicable to these phenomena limits their potential for contributing to a broad understanding of coupled systems. In this paper, we examine a variable herringbone lattice that can exhibit a wide range of applications by intentionally introducing imperfections to a simple harmonic Hamiltonian. When the Hamiltonian is disturbed from its default settings, the resulting coupled system displays a intricate transition from a simple frequency lock-in to a complex pattern of frequency multiplication and division. By employing the method of harmonic balance, we are able to analytically study the dynamics of this system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that despite its seemingly complex behavior, the system ultimately locks into a frequency that is precisely halfway between the two primary frequencies. This phenomenon holds true across varying disturbance intensities and frequencies. The approach we utilize also allows us to assess the broad spectrum of the system's power spectrum with either a narrowly focused or a broadly distributed set of frequency components. The results we obtain can be visually represented as a intricate surface that varies with time and distance along the system's parameters. The explicit inclusion of noise in addition to the disturbance perturbations reveals that noise is not a key driver of the system's complex behavior. By applying a curve-fitting technique to the surface we obtained, we are able to parameterize the system's power spectrum with just two key parameters. Ultimately, our analysis provides a clear understanding of the coupled system's dynamics and offers a practical solution for generating a wide variety of coupled oscillator systems with precisely controlled frequency ratios. The approach we utilize is applicable to a wide range of physical systems, from mechanical to optical systems. The parameterization we derived from the surface we obtained can be utilized with various coupled systems to investigate the interconnected relationships between their frequency ratios, the width of the lock-in range, and the power spectrum of the system. The relevance of our findings is demonstrated through the generation of a Jacks chain system, a commonly used example of a coupled oscillator, with a frequency ratio of 1.618, which is considered an irrational and non-regular number, but can be shown to behave similarly to the variable herringbone lattice system. The generated states are classified as catalyzed coherent states with single-photon assistance. Our analysis shows that the success probabilities of creating these states vary significantly depending on the preparation method, offering insights into the properties of hybrid quantum devices. Notably, beam splitter-prepared states exhibit unequal probability amplitudes, resulting from the hybrid nature of even and odd parities, which can be exploited for applications in quantum information, such as generating coherent single-photon entanglement for distribution in quantum networks. In contrast, the parametric amplifier produces states with the same probability amplitudes, mirroring the hybrid nature of optical parametric amplifiers, which could be useful for generating quantum entanglement for delayed distribution in quantum networks. We introduce a novel variational approach to approximating distributional objects, such as Gaussian polynomial chains, using a concise and expandable representation. This representation consists of a straightforward, easily interpretable structure that can be expanded to provide an exact, detailed approximation of the original object. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this representation by using it in an efficient variational inference method for Gaussian polynomial chains. This efficient inference method enables us to accurately approximate high-dimensional posterior distributions at a low computational cost. As a result, we can successfully infer the structural properties and parameters of Gaussian polynomial chains using only a limited number of genetic data points. Furthermore, our approach maintains the flexibility to accommodate various chain structures and can be applied to a range of related problems, such as reconstructing gene regulatory networks. We validate our approach by conducting a series of simulations that compare the accuracy of variational inference methods using traditional and expanded representations of polynomial chains. These simulations indicate that our new approach significantly improves the accuracy of variational inference, reducing the error in predicting node degrees by one order of magnitude, while also achieving a 4 orders of magnitude decrease in the elapsed time required for computation. Additionally, our approach has been successfully applied in the analysis of real data, consisting of genetic expression data from the flower species Sinningia purpurea. This analysis yields a reliable approximation of the posterior distribution of the Gaussian polynomial chain, allowing us to accurately identify protein-coding genes and the corresponding regulatory relationships. The corresponding data and software are available at https://github.com/InfPolynomics/InfPolynomics. In highly multilingual communities like Australia, NLP research has a great potential to make a significant difference. Our work focuses on developing a first-ever Australian multilingual Wikipedia knowledge graph. Our dataset consists of 20 languages and covers approximately 20 percent of Wikipedia's total content. To accomplish this, we tailored a generative model to handle multiple languages and implemented a character-level sequence generation approach to address difficulties associated with symbolic knowledge graphs. To evaluate our knowledge graph, we developed two novel metrics: a score determining the accuracy of a generated language by assessing the similarity between generated content and actual Wikipedia content, and a second score that gauges the precision of generated content in relation to original Wikipedia data. Our graph outperforms numerous competitors in both metrics when tested on multiple languages. To utilize this knowledge graph in real-world applications, we demonstrated its effectiveness in two examples: predicting a document's likely language based on its content, and generating fake documents in the same language as real ones. Our research shows that generative models can be highly effective in constructing knowledge graphs from vast amounts of multilingual data, with real-world implications for communities like Australia where language is not a barrier. The surge in visually impaired users and social media sharing has created a significant interest in accurately generating image descriptions. Presently, existing models generate precise and detailed descriptions, but often produce excess information. This phenomenon is particularly prominent in descriptions of complex scenes. Our research introduces a novel approach, called Multi-Aspect Description Generation, which produces both general and detailed descriptions of images by utilizing a hierarchical description framework. This strategy enables the model to focus on both broad and precise aspects of a scene through separate description streams. Our data expansion strategy further enhances the guidance by utilizing extended caption descriptions. We created a new evaluation metric, called Detail Ratio, to assess the generated descriptions' precision and excess information. Our experiments reveal that the proposed approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both quality and excess information, as validated by both human assessment and the newly introduced Detail Ratio evaluation metric. Our model achieves the best results on both tasks when compared to existing methods, demonstrating its superiority. Our research is publicly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github/MADG. Our findings also highlight the challenges faced in training models on large captioned data sets, such as Flickr30k, due to inconsistent caption quality. To address this issue, we developed a new data set called Fleiss30k, which incorporates exact aspect-level annotation for image description generation, making it a suitable and more precise framework than Flickr30k. The growing physical and social segregation of communities, as described by Bill Bishop in "The Big Sort," has significant implications for the dissemination of false information and the spread of polarizing ideas on social media. According to this concept, geographically isolated areas with socially homogeneous populations tend to have greater influence and more insular information flows, which can contribute to the widespread of misleading information within those communities. This phenomenon is particularly evident in areas with low population density. A recent study examines the effects of "The Big Sort" on the spread of false information through social media in the United States. The research uses Twitter data from 3,576 counties in the country and accounts for factors like population size, social media usage, and misinformation sources. The study finds that false information spreads more easily in more isolated and socially homogeneous areas, which it confirms are more influenced by local information. Moreover, the researchers distinguish between the spread of false information to new users and its retweeting among existing users, finding that "The Big Sort" facilitates both processes but especially the latter. The study also discovers that the spread of false information is more significant in rural areas with conservative populations. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the social segregation of communities can contribute substantially to the dissemination of false information and polarizing ideas through social media. The policy implications of this finding emphasize the importance of addressing social isolation and homogeneous community dynamics in addition to online interventions aimed at reducing the spread of misleading information and promoting social cohesion. The study's limitations are discussed, along with potential future research directions, such as integrating geographical and social segmentation fully and examining the relationship between the spread of false information and election outcomes. The underlying data and analysis are available for public use, offering a foundation for exploring similar research questions in the future. The code used in the analysis has also been made publicly available. To understand the underlying principles of speech-based teaching, it's necessary to examine how people express certain concepts through speech. This study has two objectives: it develops an intuitive linguistic framework for describing speech in teaching contexts and uses semantic analysis to explore the underlying concepts conveyed in speech. Researchers designed an automatic system to generate speech for various tasks and instructing specific actions, which enabled them to investigate five factors: demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, errors, and instructions. They discovered that speech conveys a range of information, including actions, relationships between actions, and goals. Furthermore, their analysis revealed that speech is influenced by the methods used to demonstrate actions, the structure of audio instructions, the presence of subtasks, and errors. This research may serve as a foundation for the development of speech-based teaching systems that utilize machine learning algorithms. Such systems will be crucial in industries such as healthcare and education, which rely heavily on human instruction. This work is an initial step towards creating speech-based teaching systems that are both efficient and effective. This research is particularly relevant to industries that deliver precise, manual procedures, such as healthcare and manufacturing, which primarily convey information through human instruction. This is because, unlike widespread claims, the actions in teaching tasks are not solely conveyed through observed demonstrations, but rather through speech that encompasses a wide range of concepts, including actions, actions in relation to each other, and goals. This is because, although observed demonstrations are crucial, they do not provide contextual information such as the purpose of acting, the order of actions, or the distinction between essential and incidental actions, which are all essential for completing tasks accurately and efficiently. This research has two primary contributions. Firstly, it develops an descriptive linguistic framework for speech in teaching contexts, revealing the underlying structure and concepts conveyed through speech. Secondly, it investigates the intricate relationship between speech and action by analyzing the semantic concepts conveyed during teaching tasks, which are influenced by various factors, including demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors. Conversational systems, found in user interfaces such as virtual assistants, pose a significant challenge to validation through automated testing frameworks. The dynamic nature of user input and the inability to predict exact interaction paths makes validation cumbersome. As a result, developers often prioritize manual testing over automated testing methods. Nonetheless, automated testing is crucial for ensuring the system's integrity, as it enables efficient and scalable testing. To address the limitations of automated testing for conversational systems, we propose a novel approach called ContextExplorer. This approach leverages a logical validation language to define test scenarios and validates the system's response to input. Furthermore, it employs a context-based exploration strategy to execute tests efficiently. Experimental evaluations reveal that ContextExplorer outperforms existing methods in terms of test execution time and coverage. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have openly sourced ContextExplorer, making it available to the development communities of various conversational system frameworks. Additionally, we provide comprehensive guidelines for integrating ContextExplorer into existing frameworks. Through ContextExplorer, we aim to streamline automated testing for conversational systems, enabling developers to focus on validation rather than testing logistics. The underlying context-based exploration strategy and logical validation framework also offer potential applications in related research domains. The context-based exploration strategy and logical validation framework underlying ContextExplorer have a broader potential impact on the scalability of automated testing for various complex systems. Medical imaging analyses often rely on neural networks, yet ensuring their consistency across different scanning modalities and patient populations remains a challenge. We investigate how training datasets with combined MRI images from different sources affect the generalization of a brain age predictor using MRI. Our analysis involves modeling brain age using a graph neural network, where we evaluate the model's performance on new, unseen MRI data. To test the generalization ability of the model regarding different scanning sources, we used a large, publicly available MRI dataset – the ADNI dataset – which includes 840 subjects with both T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery scans. We further explored the diversity of MRI datasets from different populations, including healthy adults and Alzheimer's disease patients, using the LONI CBS repository. Our results show that the model performs well in estimating the age of MRI scans from different modalities and populations, even when trained on small datasets – with a high correlation between predicted and actual ages. Furthermore, we found that the diversity of the training dataset affects the model's performance, particularly in predicting the age of older adults. When evaluating the model on scans with high cerebrovascular pathology, our results were less consistent, suggesting the need for models that can better generalize in this case. We have made the code and model predictions available for further research, contributing to the development of more robust neural networks that can handle diverse medical imaging data. Utilizing the experimental crystal structure data, we determined the band energies and electron densities for both spin configurations. Subsequent calculations of the magnetic moment per atom confirmed our observed results, revealing the compounds' non-magnetic nature in the middle composition range and the absence of an antiferromagnetic moment in Gd-rich compounds. Furthermore, we extracted the total and partial magnetic moment distributions, gaining insight into the compound's electronic structure, particularly the significant contribution of Cm atoms to the moment and the absence of moment on Gd atoms in the middle composition range. Lastly, we analyzed the possible explanations for the observed moment reversal, considering the possible effects of alloy disorder, 4f-electron hybridization, and the influence of Cm's relativistic effects, which are all supported by the DFT+U calculations. We propose that the unique alloy configuration of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds, with alternating atomic planes of Gd and Cm, contributes significantly to their magnetic properties. Deep neural network-based object detectors such as Faster RCNN and SSD have been highly effective for real-world object detection tasks including security surveillance, autonomous driving, and healthcare.  Despite their success, these models require substantial data sets to train and significant computational power for implementation.  To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, called Progressive Context Learning (PCL), that enhances the performance of low-resource object detection by progressing from simple to complex context enhancements.  The PCL framework evaluates the best object detector for a given task and application context, comparing the performance of six state-of-the-art object detection algorithms using a unified evaluation protocol.  Our research revealed that neither the most advanced nor the fastest algorithms currently existing are optimal solutions for object detection.  Rather, the PCL framework found that the best object detection algorithm depends on the specific task and application context.  Our PCL framework further presents context-adaptive enhancement modules that seamlessly integrate additional information into the detection process, significantly improving the object detection performance across various application contexts and simplifying the object detection process by eliminating the need for task-specific architecture design.  The PCL framework along with the proposed code and benchmark data is available for public access at this link: https://github.com/yu88333/PCL. Our innovative PCL framework has the potential to serve as a foundation for future object detection research and development.  Our comprehensive code and benchmark data are available for public access, facilitating straightforward replication of our research findings.  Our research proposal has been tested and validated through rigorous experiments conducted across various application contexts and simplifying the object detection process by eliminating the need for task-specific architecture design. These conditions allow us to concentrate convex functions and polynomials of these variables tightly, surpassing previous achievements. Our main conclusions can be applied to provide improved bounds for several critical probabilities in combinatorial theory, including the probability of a random graph being connected, the appearance of specific patterns in random permutations, and the occurrence of large components in random graphs. These results represent updated estimates for renowned combinatorial probabilities like $R_n$, $\mathcal{R}_n$, $f_n$, and $\rho_n$. Furthermore, our techniques involve novel applications of the Poincar\'e inequality on conditioned random variables and contribute to the development of concentration inequalities for conditioned Bernoulli random variables. These results also hold for a broader category of random variables that satisfy a certain mixing condition, often referred to as weak mixing. This condition is equivalent to variables being independent when conditioned on their sum, and it occurs frequently in random combinatorial structures, often resulting from the uniform selection of certain structures, such as random graphs, permutations, and digital sequences. In many instances, our concentration inequalities lead to precise limits for the expected value of conditioned convex functions and polynomials, thereby providing concrete bounds for various combinatorial probabilities mentioned above. We introduce a Markov Decision Process model that takes into account incompatibility as a state variable, enabling us to examine the acceptance decisions made in kidney transplant pairing. Within this framework, we seek to maximize the probability of accepting compatible donor pairs, leveraging a natural ordering inspired by lexicographic optimization. We then establish the existence of a lexicon-ordered optimal policy, leveraging Guo's theorem from 2001, and demonstrate that this policy is consistent with pairing priorities that favor higher likelihood pairs. Additionally, we derive a set of conditions under which the optimal policy exhibits a wait-or-pair strategy, akin to that observed in simple pairing models. Failing this condition, we find that the optimal policy will potentially pair the agent with a donor having a certain, lesser-quality compatibility, rather than waiting for a better match. We also develop an value function interpretation to address the policy's apparent'settlement' for an 'acceptable' pair. Furthermore, we outline the layout of future work, which will involve numerical experiments and the potential incorporation of additional factors, such as different transplant priorities. This model offers a novel framework for analyzing pair formation in the context of kidney transplantation, while also contributing a specific lexicon-ordered ordering problem that can be useful in other applications. We hope that this research will help inform policy makers and healthcare professionals about optimal transplant pairing strategies. This study examines how word embeddings misinterpret financial text vocabulary due to the lack of consideration for context, resulting in the incorrect classification of opposing terms as similar. We analyzed 13 opposing financial word pairs and found that they are often represented by distinct embeddings in a standard word2vec model. However, our data reveals significant overlap in the representation of opposing terms when considering the underlying neural language model, which can be interpreted as a manifestation of contextual antonymy. We further demonstrate how this context blindness leads to poor investment advice by recommending the purchase of stock opposing terms like 'expensive' and 'cheap', or recommending sale of stock opposing terms like'stable' and 'unstable'. To overcome this limitation, we proposed a contextualized embedding approach using a multi-step technique called path-based dynamic embedding, which captures the nuanced meanings of antonyms in financial text. This method demonstrates a significant improvement in predicting the proper classification of stock opposing term pairs like 'overvalued' and 'undervalued'. Furthermore, our results show that this approach yields contextually informed embeddings, leading to a 23.1% increase in accurate recommendations for stock opposing term pairs. Ultimately, this method can be valuable for any application involving financial text analysis that incorporates word embeddings, particularly in scenarios like stock investment decision-making. In wideband waveforming, determining optimal timing and power is crucial for enhancing data transmission efficiency and ensuring fairness among users. We developed two optimization approaches, fair-throughput and sum-throughput, using a mixed-integer convex optimization method that takes into account various constraints, including power limitations and the need to avoid interference. These optimizations can be efficiently solved using convex optimization techniques. We implemented these optimizations using the CVX library and tested them on real-world data from two different scenarios, evaluating the performance of our approach. The results showed that our fair-throughput waveforming strategy could support up to 15 users with high fairness (95%) and the sum-throughput approach could support up to 25 users with increased data transmission efficiency. Additionally, we compared our approaches with traditional fixed waveforming and observed a significant performance improvement. The research presented here is a initial step towards developing more complex waveforming strategies and presents a practical implementation example rather than an exhaustive theoretical study. The associated MATLAB code is available at Lookout Research Group website for the interest of the community in evaluating and extending the research. The fair-throughput and sum-throughput waveforming strategies we presented can be used in various applications, such as in satellite communication systems, cognitive radio networks, and multiple access systems, among others. The challenge of optimizing waveforming strategies remains a complex problem that requires further research, especially when considering delay constraints, user dynamics, and hardware limitations. We introduce a novel mechanism for multiagent learning that incorporates the concept of iteratively dominated actions, rendering it suitable for environments affected by cognitive biases. In settings plagued by bias-induced mistakes, learning agents should prioritize actions that, on average, lead to better outcomes, especially when those outcomes are yet to be experienced. To achieve this, we develop a general framework where agents receive feedback about the payoffs associated with learned actions, using this information to update their learning strategy. Specifically, we create a model where agents use a mixture of experiences, both their own and those shared by others, to guide their decision-making. Theoretical proof reveals that under certain conditions, learning actions by expediting the elimination of dominated strategies enables agents to achieve efficient equilibria more quickly. Moreover, we demonstrate that this efficient learning model precludes persistent confusion cycles, thereby ensuring that agents converge to a collaborative equilibrium. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we develop a corresponding algorithm and test it on a variety of simulated scenarios. Our results show that this algorithm succeeds in reaching efficient equilibria in even the most complex scenarios, involving large numbers of agents and extensive temporal dynamics. Our approach also compares favorably to alternative mechanisms, such as learning from observed actions, in scenarios with changing environmental conditions. Finally, we apply our model to a real-world example involving the behavior of drivers in a congested traffic pattern, using data from a actual traffic study. Our findings in this example reveal that drivers are more likely to adopt collaborative equilibria if they are allowed to learn from the experiences of others. Our approach has implications for various fields of study, including economics, transportation science, and game theory, where it may be utilized in the design of learning mechanisms that account for cognitive biases and social interaction. We've investigated a basic epidemic model where the random network changes rapidly, changing it into a configuration that resists the spread of disease. To study this, we used a Markov chain model with a highly dynamic network, ensuring the chain has a unique stationary distribution. This allowed us to identify the most resilient network setting, which we found maintains the same structure as the initial network for an extended period. To simplify the analysis, we transformed the problem into a problem of the most likely endpoint of a random walk on a dynamic network, which we compared to a model with constantly changing random connections. Our results showed that the most resilient network setting can be characterized by constantly changing connections that are uniformly likely to change in either direction, which we confirmed through numerical simulations. Furthermore, this model provided insights into the dynamics of network changes, revealing how the rate of network changes affects the spread of the epidemic, literally changing the number of people infected, which we demonstrated through numerical simulations. Our most basic model could be extended to represent different epidemic scenarios by introducing random connections between specific groups of people. Our findings revealed that the most resilient network setting can be affected by the presence of isolated individuals, the presence of health experts, or time limits for connection maintenance, which we also validated through numerical simulations. Ultimately, our model provided a framework for understanding the dynamics of network changes in relation to the spread of epidemics, as well as offering practical guidelines for the implementation of successful containment measures. Our approach also introduced a novel approach to addressing first passage chain problems on dynamic networks. Our most basic model has been made available as software through the software repository. We introduce the variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework, a general method that refines policy gradient estimates through experience replay, and show that policy gradient reinforcement learning with experience replay fits within this overall framework, resulting in an enhanced estimator with reduced variance. We then derive a specific variance-reduced estimator for simple policy gradient methods, and demonstrate the efficacy of these variants through numerical experiments on well-known benchmark problems. Numerical experiments confirm the superior performance of variance-reduced estimators. Furthermore, we analyze the theoretical variance of our proposed estimator and compare it to existing results, also showing that the VarRG estimator achieves the optimal variance when selecting the optimal experience replay ratio. We also provide guidelines on choosing the optimal experience replay ratio, both analytically and numerically, and offer the variance-reduced estimator as a handy tool for the community. Our code is now publicly available, allowing easy incorporation of the variance-reduced estimator into the practice of reinforcement learning experts. Although we focus on policy gradient methods, we show in the appendix that variance reduction can be applied to value-function-based methods as well, offering a general framework that can be tailored to various experience replay-based reinforcement learning algorithms. We also propose a possible extension to the current framework for addressing policy regularization in reinforcement learning. We anticipate that the introduced variance-reduced experience replay framework will serve as a starting point for the further improvement of reinforcement learning methods employing experience replay. A key aspect of conversational AI involves generating relevant dialogue based on initial statements. To achieve this, the underlying assumption is that the system possesses a basic understanding of the other party's mental state, specifically the ability to recognize unexpressed thoughts and intentions. To investigate this, a simple generative model was developed which generates dialogue that considers the listener's unexpressed thoughts. To evaluate the system's ability to mimic this kind of dialogue, a dataset was created consisting of dialogue generated using the model, as well as variations of the same dialogue generated without considering the listener's unexpressed thoughts. Human evaluators were then tasked with identifying which of the dialogue variants was more plausible. The analysis of their responses showed that the majority of evaluators preferred the more sophisticated dialogue, indicating that even a limited theory of mind can play a significant role in generating convincing and human-like dialogue. Moreover, by comparing different models, it was demonstrated that the inclusion of theory of mind in a generative model leads to a greater increase in dialogue understanding than in a simpler generative dialog model. Finally, by conducting an acceptance test on dialogue generated with and without theory of mind, it was found that the former was considered more credible by users. The dataset used in this research has been made available for public use. The goal of future work is hoped to be building upon this research by incorporating a richer theory of mind into the model, potentially leading to a more comprehensive understanding of how theory of mind affects dialog generation, as well as exploring alternative methods of evaluating the credibility of generated dialogue. To accelerate the evaluation of gravitational forces in simulations involving large numbers of bodies, a novel algorithm called MG-GLAM is presented, which is based on a combination of multigrid methods and hierarchical amplitude estimation and works in its most efficient form in 3D space. Unlike other multigrid codes, MG-GLAM utilizes a unique combination of fundamental lookup tables to determine potential values, significantly boosting the code's efficiency by approximately ten times relative to its previous iteration, while also offering precise results with minimal error. The development of MG-GLAM began as a project to improve the FAUST N-body integration code and resulted in a code that can handle up to 500 million bodies on a single computer within a 24-hour time frame, or sustain the integration of 10 million bodies for a longer period of time. The advantages of MG-GLAM are particularly evident in scenarios with wide distance distributions and dense cluster formations, where it exhibits a linear improvement in performance over earlier versions. We introduce the chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$) as a way to extend SLE$_\kappa$ within the complex plane, and find that it consists of curves that grow infinitely as time progresses, accompanied by the creation of discrete, branching points of order $\kappa$ over time. When $\kappa$ equals 4, these branches transform into multiple origins of the complex plane, each of which gives rise to a line segment growing infinitely as time goes on. We also establish that the resulting system resembles the radial Schramm-Loewner evolution (rSLE) with $\kappa=4$ but with an "imaginary surface" $\mathcal{P}$ defined by branching points mapped through the inverse flow, and we prove that the system resolves the surface $\mathcal{P}$ into multiple planes separated by growing line segments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that rSLE can be obtained from SLE$_\kappa$ with $0\leq \kappa<8$ by introducing a random clock, and also establish that the resulting system corresponds to the radial Schramm-Loewner evolution with the addition of an "imaginary surface" $\mathcal{P}$, with multiple planes connected by growing line segments. We further investigate the relationship between SLE$_\kappa$, the resulting system, and the Loewner equation, and also explore the connection between SLE$_\kappa$ with $0\leq \kappa<8$ and the radial Schramm-Loewner evolution. Moreover, we derive the existence and uniqueness of the system evolved from SLE$_\kappa$ with $0\leq \kappa<8$, as well as the same system evolved from the radial Schramm-Loewner evolution. We also establish that the resulting system corresponds to the Dolgopolov theorem about the branching points of the imaginary surface $\mathcal{P}$. We introduce WorkingWiki, a fully-automated system designed to simplify the collaboration on scientific manuscripts and software by leveraging a wiki platform. WorkingWiki can identify the project components needed for collaboration and move them to separate repositories for development and publication, thereby enabling seamless separation of temporary content from permanent content. Additionally, it incorporates a automatic publisher that is aware of the underlying structure and ensures that the wiki pages adhering to standard documentation formats can be easily compiled into publication-ready documents, without the need for additional configuration. We demonstrate the benefits of WorkingWiki through a real-world example involving the development of the ARK ontology toolset and the corresponding working paper on WorkingWiki, showcasing how it facilitates successful collaboration on both software and associated scientific publications. The resulting paper and software code enjoy a clean separation of content, facilitating successful publication and software dissemination. The WorkingWiki approach can be applied to any wiki-based project. The underlying system and methodology for WorkingWiki are fully open-source, as evidenced by its availability on GitHub at https://github.com/leibnizkwk/WorkingWiki. We invite the scientific community to adopt and further develop WorkingWiki. We also present the ARK Ontology Editor 2.0, a significant upgrade to the existing ARK Ontology Editor 1.0, featuring improved support for sub-corpus markup, alongside various usability enhancements, and is now deployable at https://ark-data.org/editor. The corresponding methodology for DevelopingWiki has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/leibnizkwk/DevelopingWiki. We investigate the implications of ultralight dark matter, potentially explaining the observed cosmic anomaly, on the behavior of neutrinos within a unified framework that includes a dark sector. Using a semi-analytical approach, we examine the dynamics of neutrinos within the ultralight dark matter field in various scenarios. As the density of the dark matter field adjusts, we observe adjustments in the neutrino effective mass, density fluctuations, and the formation of neutrino streams. Furthermore, we assess the impact of neutrinos on the ultralight dark matter phase transition, probing the robustness of this transition in relation to neutrino oscillations and their own interactions. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting signatures of this theory, including the creation of neutrino self-interference patterns, the formation of neutrino streams, and the effects of the dark matter field on neutrino fluctuations during the early universe, which could be evident through upscattered background photons in the near infrared/solar neutrino spectrum. Finally, we discuss possible connections to the observed cosmic anomaly and the potential for future research. This study paves the way for a comprehensive numerical solution to the problem. This research is a preliminary step towards understanding the interconnection between neutrinos and the ultralight dark matter sector, encouraging further investigation into the dynamics of this combined system. This is the first study to explore the dynamics of neutrinos within the ultralight dark matter field, revealing the interrelated effects on each other and uncovering the embedded neutrino interactions within the ultralight dark matter field that influence the early universe. This is the first time the neutrino effective mass, the formation of neutrino streams, the neutrino self-interference patterns, the neutrino fluctuations during the early universe, the solar neutrino excess, and the ultralight dark matter particle physics are integrated into a unified framework. This is also the first study to probe the robustness of the ultralight dark matter phase transition in relation to neutrino oscillations and their own interactions, explore the potential for detecting signatures of this theory, and discuss the possible connections to the observed cosmic anomaly. This is the first time the formation of neutrino streams during the early universe, the creation of neutrino self-interference patterns, the effects of the dark matter field on neutrino fluctuations during the early universe, and the solar neutrino excess are proposed to be related to each other and the ultralight dark matter field. The nonlocal gravity theory has been modified to improve the confidence in its validity, and this updated version has been applied to investigate the behavior of vector perturbations in the atmospheres of black wounds. Notably, the new constitutive relation yields a significant change in the absorption of vector perturbations, specifically those related to the multipole moments of scalar particles and photons, which, in turn, leads to a notable shift in the mass function from $1/r^2$ and becomes $r^2$ for a particular type of perturbation. Additionally, the characteristic time needed for vector perturbations to be absorbed by the nonlocal gravity also shifts from $r/c_{\rm ph}$ to $r^2/c_{\rm ph}$, where $c_{\rm ph}$ is the photon speed. Moreover, the new regime in which the most general relativistic oscillations around black wounds are described results in a change from an exponential cut-off to a power-law cut-off, with possible implications for the high-energy particle physics experiments that might be able to detect quark and gluon fields in the nonlocal gravity theory. Moreover, a comparison with the standard local gravity, as described by Einstein's general theory of relativity, reveals that the characteristic length scale associated with the nonlocal gravity, roughly in the order of $10^{-33}$ cm, is too small to be detectable through the observation of black wound atmospheres, yet it was found that the nonlocal gravity can affect the behavior of primordial gravitational waves generated during the early universe, which, in turn, could impact the nonlocal gravity's potential for consistency with the laws of quantum gravity. Furthermore, the new nonlocal gravity constitutive relation also influences the formation of primordial black wounds and affects the probability of their formation, with possible implications for the likelihood of detecting gravitational waves produced by the collapse of primordial black wounds. The research on nonlocal gravity's impact on the atmosphere of black wounds also leads to the development of a new method for calculating the decay rates of particle decays induced by the nonlocal gravity. To better understand how genetic information from sequence influences phenotypic associations, we developed a novel approach that accurately predicts SNPs associated with traits despite limited direct access to genotype data. Many important concepts in graph theory, such as matching and bichromatic 2-dimensional crosscing, can be expressed through bipartite graphs. These applications often require these bipartite graphs to be planar, meaning the graph can be drawn on a two-dimensional surface without edge crossings. This paper addresses the problem of determining whether a given bipartite graph can be split into two subgraphs through vertex separation, such that both subgraphs have planar drawings and there is no edge between them. This is equivalent to finding the maximum number of edges in a subgraph that can be separated from the rest of the bipartite graph while allowing for vertex separation. This paper establishes an algorithm that achieves this maximum by examining all possible vertex separations in a linear order, which ensures the subgraph in question can be drawn planarly. This algorithm's efficiency is measured by a parameter called the minimum degree, which serves as a key factor in determining the subgraph's edge count. This paper further explores specific cases of bipartite graphs, notably complete graphs and regular graphs, providing more tailored solutions. These solutions demonstrate the feasibility of splitting specific graph types, while also offering statistical analysis. This paper investigates the formal power series field, $k[(x)]$, over an infinite field $k$ and determines the decidability of the theory of this field under its standard residue map, particularly for the characteristic zero case. Building on Theorem 1.1, which shows that the theory of $k[(x)]$ with standard residue map is undecidable for any infinite field $k$, we argue that this implies an infinite field $k$ cannot have a decidable theory when it comes to its power series field $k[(x)]$ equipped with a total residue map. Consequently, we deduce that an infinite field $k$ cannot have a decidable theory when it comes to its power series field $k[(x)]$ with a total residue map, as this would contradict the result found in Theorem 1.1. Furthermore, we establish that both the theory of $k[(x)]$ and the total residue map are undecidable for any infinite field $k$. This expands upon a previous ruling against the decidability of the theory of random graph $G_3$ by incorporating a more general framework, and thereby providing an alternative proof of its undecidability. Moreover, we also prove that neither the field $k$ nor the field $k[(x)]$ have a computable theory for any infinite field $k$. Ultimately, we demonstrate that neither the field $\mathfrak{F}_1$ nor the field $\mathfrak{F}_2$ have a decidable or computable theory. This research is an extension of the work done in by Dolazhbkov at the 2015 mathematical logic conference in Minsk. We also build on the results from our previous paper with Goloviera at the 2015 mathematical logic conference in Minsk, with discussions on the decidability of certain first-order theories involving formal power series fields. In the context of vertical federated learning, users share their data with a central server for machine learning model training, which is increasingly popular due to data protection constraints. However, our research reveals significant vulnerabilities in two widely used privacy protocols: rectangular protocol and exponential protocol. By manipulating training data and the machine learning model, we showed that an attacker can successfully launch a price-inflation attack, a privacy-aware attack, and a regression attack that enables them to compromise security and privacy. Furthermore, we developed a new attack that allows us to guess specific data items, demonstrating that confidence intervals originally proposed to prevent data inflation are actually ineffective. To resolve these issues, we proposed an attack-detecting mechanism and a new exponential protocol with a robust attack-resistant parameter, significantly improving the efficiency of the original protocol while ensuring the confidentiality of the data. Our approach and protocol enhancements provide a foundation for investigating other protocol customizations. A fundamental challenge in protoplanetary disk research arises from the discrepancy between the small scales required for planetesimals to form and the larger scales observed for gas and solids. A key aspect of overcoming this difficulty involves incorporating substructures into models of protoplanetary disks. In this study, we examine the formation of vortex-like substructures, specifically in the context of external solar nebula radiation, and evaluate their capacity to contribute to planetesimal formation through gravitational settling. By simulating a type A migration scenario and modeling the behavior of solid particles subject to radial wind forces, we found that substructures in the form of vortices form in the upper regions of accretion disks. These vortices exhibit long lifetimes, potentially millions of years, and their scales align with the requirements for planetesimal formation. We also observed that the formation of these vortices is concentrated near the snow line and above, where the temperature allows for the presence of ice, and their occurrence rate is estimated to be approximately 10-100 vortices per solar mass per year. This occurs due to the settling of solid particles within the vortices, with the smallest particles settling fastest, and the formation of a dense, solid-rich core at the center of each vortex. We propose a model for their evolution, in which they develop a certain level of width before the Settling Barrier and then maintain a constant width for millions of years. This width matches the scale needed to form planetesimals through gravitational settling. We also consider alternative scenarios for their formation and destruction and find that core cooling and the formation of dense cores at their centers could potentially prevent the formation of planets from the solids within them. This study provides a possible solution to the planet formation problem in protoplanetary disks and suggests that planets may form through the settling of solids within vortices in disk substructures. This could also explain the characteristics of certain exoplanets, such as Kepler-36's compact, close-in configuration and the presence of small rocky planets inside the habitable zone of low-mass stars like KOI-423. This study paves the way for future work on the evolution of these substructures and the formation of planets within them through numerical simulations of protoplanetary disk evolution. Our analysis reveals that optimal robustness is achieved with frequency deviations that match the spacing between adjacent ions, leading to a sustained, delayed onset of entanglement as well as its eventual saturation. In contrast, implementing precise target frequencies or using unwanted multiplexing can result in impaired entanglement generation across broader spectral ranges, thereby indicating the value of designing robust gates with broad spectral tolerance for use in variational algorithms that require abundant entanglement formation over extensive ion chains. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates can successfully generate ample entanglement even at frequencies far removed from optimal conditions, leveraging the robust properties of dipolar interactions within ion chains. This research focuses on HNL decay into a light neutrino and a charged lepton, where the light neutrino leads to a missing energy signature. 3D face reconstruction is a well-known issue in computer vision and graphics. Many methods exist that incorporate both pose-dependent and pose-independent elements to generate a 3D face. These approaches often rely on regression networks that produce face coordinates. A novel proposal, the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), is presented in this paper.  SARNet consists of two separate networks for estimating pose-independent and pose-dependent factors. These networks are designed to operate independently and do not share variables during training. The paper also introduces a new loss function, the Self-aligned Dual Loss (SADL), which evaluates the distance between predicted and actual face points from various angles. Experimental data from the facial point cloud reconstruction dataset (FPR) and the Scenewalk dataset demonstrate that SARNet achieves better results compared to existing methods. The paper also visualizes a reconstructed 3D face at varied angles to showcase the efficacy of this new approach. The code for SARNet is available online at a specified repository path.

We're investigating the impact of a positive adiabatic index on the evolution of the Bardeen potential during inflationary phases, specifically when the scalar power spectrum results in large negative Bardeen potential values. Initially, we'll establish the relationship between the Bardeen potential and the scalar field in an idealized, power-law inflationary model. Subsequently, we'll examine a more general scenario with positive $\phi$ driving a scalar field, using a perturbative approach to analyze the effects of small $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_2$ on the Bardeen potential. Furthermore, we'll use approximate solutions to the full Einstein-Boltzmann system, combining the dynamics of the Bardeen potential and the scalar field. We provide new formulas for the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees and marked ordered trees. The proof involves integrating the highest node function over the set of standard ordered trees or marked ordered trees, treated as a stochastic process. This approach enables us to derive explicit formulas for the expected value of the highest node, as well as its variance and higher moments. The formula for the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees can be compared to a previous result, and the formula for marked ordered trees is new. The moment formula also allows us to determine the standard deviation of the highest node in standard ordered trees or marked ordered trees. The investigation of these moments can be viewed as an application of the highest score problem to enumerative combinatorial analysis. The method used to obtain these results can be extended to calculate the moments of the highest node in the conditional uniform distribution over the set of standard ordered trees or marked ordered trees with a given number of nodes, resulting in a moment formula that is more complex. The standard deviation of the highest node in standard ordered trees or marked ordered trees can be compared to their respective depths, and the investigation of this ratio leads to an analysis of the distribution of the highest node in its range, which is shown to be asymptotically approximately exponential for large numbers of nodes. The research into the distribution of the highest node in its range also enables the examination of its connection to the extreme value theory, specifically the extension of the extreme value theorem to combinatorial contexts. The investigation of the ratio of the highest node to its range provides an understanding of the variability of the highest node and can be related to the maximum of independent random variables, which is a fundamental problem in stochastic combinatorial analysis. The methods developed in this research can be applied to the analysis of other combinatorial contexts involving composable objects, which are studied as a result of applying functions to their properties. Accurate optical character recognition in vote tabulation relies on a spell checker. We created a novel spell correction algorithm for this purpose by modifying the Levenstein distance metric to better suit the optical character recognition errors it addresses. This distance metric change reduces the algorithm's complexity from a non-deterministic polynomial time (NP) to a polynomial time, enabling it to be part of a larger package that can be efficiently compiled and executed without requiring multiple iterations. We tested this algorithm on a dataset of handwritten votes and compared it to two other spell correction algorithms, achieving a 15% higher correction rate. We also demonstrated that employing word-level Levenstein distance yields a correction rate 20% higher than the standard word-level spell checker approach. This efficient spell checker was subsequently incorporated into the TabVote system, which encompasses several features including a spell checker, a Levenstein distance calculator, a voter roll checker, and a Borda count ballot interpreter. We tested this system on 21 real-world datasets and found it to be 90% effective in correctly interpreting up to 99.8% of handwritten votes, with the remaining 10% being a 1.5% error rate that requires human intervention to correct. This system can be compiled on standard hardware and software platforms, and the source code is freely available to ensure transparency and facilitate customization based on specific requirements. We also presented three different word-level Levenstein distance algorithms and compared their efficiency and effectiveness. In addition to the Levenstein distance metric, we experimented with the Hamming distance metric on this dataset, found it to be less effective, and thus advocated for the Levenstein distance metric as the standard approach for this specific application. In linear model training, data dimensions can increase unlimitedly as the number of data points grows, especially when input variables are allowed to change over time and new observations are continually added, potentially making the data infinite-dimensional. Classic statistical approaches often break down in such dynamic settings, but recent findings show that, under certain conditions, infinite-dimensional data can be accurately represented using a finite number of parameters. This research develops two linear model training algorithms that handle infinite-dimensional data through the use of a dimensionality indicator, which is itself a function of time, and includes an interesting special case where the indicator function eventually becomes negligible in the space of infinite dimensions. The first algorithm, designed for models with fixed indicator dimensions at every time point, utilizes a unique technique called 'lifting' to analyze its performance, thereby offering theoretical insights into the conditions necessary for accurate representation. This knowledge is applied to evolve linear models with time-dependent indicators, providing a benchmark against which the second algorithm is compared. The second algorithm, tailored for models with changing indicator dimensions over time, is numerically shown to achieve better performance than the first algorithm in a specific scenario. Both algorithms are evaluated using synthetic data, and the dimensions of the indicator function are explored in depth. This research was motivated by an analysis of a specific linear model application known as the 'heterogeneous dynamic matrix factorization model'. It also introduces three new datasets with large data dimensions, which are currently unlimited, although the research suggests they may become finite in the future. This study demonstrates how over-parameterized linear models can be efficiently trained on an unlimited amount of data when the condition of infinite data dimensions is met over a finite period of time. This finding is illustrated using both synthetic and real dataset examples. This research builds upon prior work done on the topic by providing a new model and three previously unreported datasets. It also presents two algorithmic solutions to train linear models with infinite data dimensions, which can become finite in the future, and evaluates these algorithms using the previously unreported datasets. This research addresses the challenge of training linear models when data dimensions increase unlimitedly, which can happen in time-dependent settings, and explores the possibility of finite dimensions in the future. As risk-management becomes increasingly vital in electricity storage operations, incorporating uncertainty is crucial for optimal storage policy and management. Our research identifies the storage industry's risk-seeking or risk-averse nature and explains how this behavior impacts policies aimed at reducing carbon emissions. We find that risk-averse storage operators prioritize short-term profitability, which may result in storage units being underutilized, especially during peak pricing events. Furthermore, we determine the optimal risk level and storage policy, taking into account technology costs, performance, and risk preferences, as well as electricity price fluctuations and temperature effects on consumption. Our results suggest that storage risk preferences influence the industry's learning rate and optimal storage capacity, and that policies such as risk management and renewable portfolio standards can mitigate storage risk and accelerate industry learning. Ultimately, our study provides a framework for evaluating the efficacy of policies and risk-management strategies on the performance of electricity storage systems. Our evaluation and analysis are illustrated through an empirical application using data from the California market. We also discuss the generalizability of our approach to other markets sharing similar characteristics. Finally, we outline potential pathways for future research on this topic. Our findings and approach are relevant to policy-makers and industry regulators in regions with electricity storage systems in place or planned for implementation in the near future. We demonstrate the applicability of our methodology using a specific empirical example, yet the underlying analysis is market-agnostic, allowing for easy adaptation to other market frameworks. Our research stems from the following broader background: although electricity storage systems offer significant benefits for risk management and renewable energy integration, the lack of actionable knowledge on storage risk preferences hinders policy-making in this field. Consequently, our study generates new knowledge on storage risk preferences and explores its implications for policy design, filling this existing research gap. Ultimately, our approach and findings provide a foundation for evaluating and comparing risk-management strategies and policies affecting storage systems in various markets. Our most recent update includes a revised analysis of storage system learning rates in California. Moreover, our research has been cited in recent studies examining the risk preferences of individual households rather than storage systems. Additionally, our approach has been utilized in recent research on optimal risk-management strategies for storage systems in the presence of curved risk preferences, and in another study that investigated the learning rates of storage systems in the Eastern United States. This study investigates the behavior of an idealized baroclinic storm on Mars within a computer-simulated Earth-like atmosphere. Our model incorporates an elliptical shape to represent the storm's influence and allows for the inclusion of an atmospheric circulation pattern known as the "polar jet." By simulating the storm's development within this model, we observed similarities between its behavior and that of the Earth's North Atlantic Oscillation. Furthermore, the storm exhibited a pattern of circulation that reversed seasonally, mirroring the behavior of the Martian polar jet. By analyzing these results, we gained insight into the factors that influence the storm's development, including the temperature contrast between the planet's poles and its midlatitudes, the strength of the polar jet, and the presence of persistent high-pressure systems on the planet. Overall, our model suggests that baroclinic storms on Mars are a natural consequence of the planet's circulation patterns and temperature differences, and could play a significant role in the transport of dust on the planet. Additionally, these storms may also affect the planet's seasonal climate variability, particularly in regions far from the equator. Notably, our model predicts that the application of the beta-plane approximation, a simplified model of the curvature of a planet, can be effectively used to simulate these storms on Mars. This study provides a foundation for future research into the baroclinic storms on Mars within a more complex model that includes the effects of the planet's polar ice caps and dust atmosphere. Most existing active learning methods are straightforward, selecting the most uncertain samples for labeling based on confidence scores. Although these techniques yield efficient performance on modest-scale datasets like MNIST and Fashion MNIST, they fall short on larger, more complex datasets like ImageNet due to inconsistent results and poor generalization. In our study, we investigate the underlying dynamics affecting the effectiveness of active learning and emphasize the significance of considering dataset nuances to make reliable, precise predictions. Our research explores various frameworks, such as confidence, diversity, and a combined method, and reveals that many uncertainties currently inherent in active learning theory are unlikely to be resolved until more precise model performance is achieved. To demonstrate our findings, we conduct extensive experiments on popular benchmark datasets, incorporating both graph-based and neural network-based examples, and our results reveal that many of the existing methods, in fact, the current active learning theory, are significantly inferior to random sampling, our proposed solution aims to fill this significant gap in active learning methodology. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/SimpleActiveLearning. Our work ultimately highlights the need for a more critical examination of active learning theory and the development of more advanced methods that can effectively support the supervision of large-scale datasets. Our findings also reveal that model reliability greatly influences the effectiveness of active learning and provide a robust evaluation framework for assessing the usability of various methods and datasets. Our research encourages the community to participate in an extensive examination of active learning theory and its practical applications. Quantum computing based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in silicon can potentially excel due to robust control and two-qubit logic capabilities. The effectiveness of this approach depends heavily on the placement and tuning of donor atoms, which, when combined with the silicon substrate, allow for precise manipulation of the surrounding electronic states. In the case of Heisenberg-lattice implementations, specifically with a dimer structure, we found that donor atoms at particular tuned phases can create stable two-qubit logic gates, with some varying in accuracy from 99.5 to 99.9%. Furthermore, we observed that changing the position of donor atoms also alters the coherence time of the system. Additionally, our analysis indicates that placing donor atoms based solely on their position is not sufficient, but rather they must be aligned with the electronic states of the Heisenberg lattice. Moreover, our proposed scheme offers scope for further improvement in the efficiency of two-qubit logic gates, with possible optimizations in donor placement, device design, and coherent control protocols. Our research utilizes a combination of theoretical models and experimental NMR data.
