The behavior of electric resistance at low magnetic field strengths in bulk semiconductor samples is highly complex and requires further exploration. In particular, the dynamics of the zeroth Landau level, which shows resistant oscillations in macroscopic quantities, are not well understood and have not been adequately studied in bulk semiconductors. However, research on GaAs/Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$As quantum wells reveals a well-defined zero Landau level resistance peak that has not been observed in bulk semiconductors and provides a more in-depth examination of scattering processes within the quantum wells. By examining the peak resistance through theoretical modeling, researchers have identified the scattering processes that dominate the zero Landau level behavior. Furthermore, investigations into edge disorder and its impact on the resistance peak reveal a transitional phase where the peak resistance is governed by a power law in relation to magnetic field strength, exhibiting edge disorder's substantial influence on the zero Landau level behavior. Nonetheless, despite this behavior being observed in bulk semiconductors, the peak resistance returns to its initial state when scattering processes are dominated by spin-orbit interactions. Moreover, research on intrinsic zero Landau level scattering processes within the quantum wells offers a comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics of the zeroth Landau level behavior. Nonetheless, edge effects and scattering processes will continue to impact the zero Landau level behavior in semiconductor-based devices, presenting fundamental limitations that must be considered in the design of magnetic field-based technologies. Nonetheless, understanding the zero Landau level behavior through research on GaAs/Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$As quantum wells may also uncover new aspects of scattering processes within the zero Landau level that could potentially be utilized in technology development. Furthermore, the power law relation that edge disorder exhibits with power law index $p \approx 1.46$ could be an universal characteristic of zero Landau level behavior in semiconductor-based devices. A dynamic TDD system is proposed where, based on channel conditions, certain bands shift between uplink and downlink to maximize throughput. Determining optimal power allocation and scheduling in such a system becomes a complex problem. To address this issue, a new algorithm is developed for power allocation and scheduling in dynamic TDD systems, leveraging the proposal's flexibility to change the direction of data transmission. To improve efficiency, a new criterion is introduced, allowing for faster convergence when determining the optimal power allocation and scheduling. To validate the algorithm's effectiveness, simulations were conducted, revealing significant improvements in throughput when comparing the proposed algorithm to existing approaches, including up to 30% better results in certain scenarios. Additionally, through simulation, factors such as variable traffic patterns and mobile patterns were tested to ensure the algorithm's robustness. A theoretical analysis was also conducted to better understand the proposed algorithm's properties and performance. Overall, the proposed solution provides a efficient and effective solution for power allocation and scheduling in dynamic TDD systems. A software tool was also developed to test the algorithm in real-world settings, consisting of a simulator for dynamic TDD systems, an evaluator for performance metrics, and a commander to manage simulation settings, all integrated into one framework known as DTTSIM. To ensure fairness in comparisons, the proposed algorithm was compared to established methods, including RL, GOA, and MAX-TH, through various tests. The resulting data were analyzed to determine the optimal threshold for switching between uplink and downlink modes in dynamic TDD systems. Finally, the limitations of the proposed solution are recognized, including the assumption of fixed priority rules and the challenge of implementing a faster power allocation algorithm while ensuring fairness in data transmission. To achieve the best possible performance in dynamic TDD systems, guidance is provided on desired features for power allocation and scheduling algorithms, including the ability to adapt quickly to changing environments and prioritize certain data transmissions over others. The framework developed in this research remains viable for future system improvements, given the constant evolution of wireless communication systems. The proposed algorithm and simulation framework are available for download, offering a foundation for ongoing research in this area, and the resulting data have been made available for public use, consisting of 21 datasets generated under different test scenarios. We propose a novel collaborative machine learning framework known as Trust-based Multi-agent Learning, in which a group of autonomous agents works together to enhance the accuracy of their machine learning models and earn a high trust score. Within this framework, each agent is assigned a unique role and can choose from two possible actions: collaborating with other agents or working independently. We then develop a mathematical model to guide the behavior of agents based on their reputation and establish the conditions under which cooperation leads to both a higher trust score and higher precision in machine learning. Furthermore, we introduce an incentive mechanism tailored to an open, decentralized environment and test our proposed framework in two scenarios: one in which agents already possess a certain level of trust and one in which there is no initial trust established. Our results show that this framework results in higher accurate machine learning models and higher trust scores in both cases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the trust score and model accuracy follow optimal paths as they develop over time. We also investigate the theoretical limits of this framework and provide a quantitative analysis of its optimal performance. A working demonstration of our proposed framework is available at https://tvmegacorp.github.io/TVMEL/. This demonstration includes the code and tutorials for using the TVME-L library in various machine learning tasks using Python. This framework and the associated repository prove particularly useful for applications in that trust and cooperation are crucial factors, such as crowdsourcing and internet of things systems. We anticipate that this framework and the associated repository will also be valuable for the teaching of various topics, including game theory, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. We have made the code and tutorials for these teachings available at https://tvmegacorp.github.io/TVMEL/. This code and set of tutorials can be used with the following courses: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Introduction to Machine Learning, Game Theory and Artificial Intelligence, Crowdsourcing and Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence. This motivates the exploration of a twisted link theory using $J_n^T$. A more efficient method is proposed, along with a step-to-step guide for calculating the $J_n^T$ polynomial specifically for volume-like twisted links. This approach leverages the volume-like representation to facilitate the computation. This paper also illustrates the application of the $J_n^T$ polynomial to a non-trivial, twisted link example. This example demonstrates the utility of the $J_n^T$ polynomial in providing a clear, graphical representation of a twisted link. This representation enables the straightforward computation of the $J_n^T$ polynomial. This computation reveals an intriguing pattern, indicating that the $J_n^T$ polynomial values are directly linked to the number of specific crossing types within the twisted link. This observation is demonstrated for a particular case study of a volume-like twisted link. This research opens up future possibilities for investigating the $J_n^T$ polynomial in more comprehensive and generalized contexts. This involves examining the $J_n^T$ polynomial for various types of links, including twisted links with multiple components and twisted chains with gaps. This study also lays the groundwork for exploring other polynomial invariants, such as the $L$-polynomial, for twisted links. This could potentially lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying mathematics and properties of these polynomials. This approach could also facilitate the comparison of different polynomial invariants for twisted links. This comparison could, in turn, provide valuable insights into the theoretical foundations of these polynomials. This research demonstrates the practical utility of the $J_n^T$ polynomial in a real-world application, specifically in the computation of the $J_n^T$ polynomial for a non-trivial, volume-like twisted link. This achievement is accompanied by an notable observation, revealing that the $J_n^T$ polynomial values are directly related to the number of specific crossing types within the twisted link. This study provides an examination of the top quark pair production cross section in 7 and 8 TeV p p collisions based on a 20.3 inverse picoboise strong signal in the full ATLAS dataset from 2012. The research focuses on events featuring one or two charged leptons to analyze the process, considering the relevant backgrounds for events with two leptons. In a database system, accuracy is crucial, and we classifies errors into two categories: those requiring complete database knowledge and those that can be determined without it. To address this problem, we propose a novel approach that compares expected outcomes with actual ones, which generates accurate results even when the database is unknown. To accomplish this, we develop a framework that utilizes a contrast learning algorithm, produces predictions that are accurate in both the presence and absence of complete database knowledge, and outperforms existing benchmarks according to our experiments. Furthermore, our framework addresses class imbalance issues, achieves significant improvement over existing solutions, and provides actionable insights into the decision-making process. Our research demonstrates the proposed approach's versatility, as it can be applied to various applications, including hate speech detection, sentiment analysis, and binary classification of medical data. This research investigates the difficulty of privacy breach computation in differentially private training for graphs, specifically focusing on learning node representations in graph-based classification tasks. Initially, a private algorithm is proposed to classify graphs based on node labels, and then the difficulty of estimating a sensitive node's attribute is quantified using the interconnectivity of graph structure. The results indicate that the difficulty of this estimation grows exponentially in relation to the number of connections in the graph, providing insight into why graph-based classification generally suffers from high privacy breaches, often exceeding those of list-based tasks. Furthermore, an analytical framework is established to evaluate the privacy loss in relation to the difficulty of estimating hidden node attributes, and this is demonstrated in a controlled environment using synthetic data. Additionally, an empirical study is conducted using real-world data, involving the publication of fake graphs constructed from a set of hidden class labels, the recruitment of participants to classify these graphs, and finally the comparison of different scenarios for publishing training data. The objectives of these experiments are (1) to measure the privacy loss in relation to the difficulty of estimating hidden class labels and (2) to evaluate the accuracy of a differentially private classifier for a node label that was previously kept hidden during the training phase, using various publication scenarios of training data. The results show that the difficulty of estimating hidden class labels exceeds the difficulty of estimating a random list element by up to 24 times, and also shows the accuracy of a differentially private classifier for a node label that was previously kept hidden during the training phase can be as low as 0.16, depending on the classification task and the publication strategy of training data. The research concludes by highlighting the challenges of applying differentially private algorithms to graph-based classification tasks and identifying potential future work, such as developing private algorithms that can learn from interconnective data and evaluating the privacy losses in other machine learning tasks for graph-based data, including node representation learning and graph classification. Bucket Elimination (BE) is a fundamental inference and optimization technique on graphical models, specifically designed to compute marginal queries by breaking them down into sub-problems on smaller subsets of variables. Despite BE's significance, the standard approach to implementing BE has a major shortcoming, as it requires significant additional computational effort compared to other methods, being particularly costly when performing optimization tasks or combining small sub-problems. In response to these limitations, we present a novel algorithm called Optimistic BE (OpBE), which not only enhances the efficiency of BE by employing an optimistic approach but also leverages this strategy to mitigate the need for additional computations during inference and optimization. Furthermore, OpBE is shown to employ a same structure of computation as other methods, enabling it to combine the results efficiently and effectively, resulting in a more general and more efficient framework than previous BE implementations. We have formally proven that OpBE is not only more efficient than the standard BE approach but also provides the same output, and it is also shown to be a generalization of existing methods, including recent optimization algorithms, which only represent specific instances of OpBE. We have tested OpBE on various synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its enhanced performance and scalability in comparison to the standard BE approach and other methods. In addition to the algorithm itself, we have also developed OpBE further to enhance its scalability, resulting in OpBE-GC, which we have rigorously evaluated to determine the best set of parameters to use in order to achieve the largest set of applicable queries while maintaining minimal additional computational expense. In contrast to the original OpBE algorithm, which is suited to single-threaded computation, we have also introduced a parallelization technique for OpBE-GC, which we have tested on large-scale datasets consisting of millions of variables and buckets. With the development of OpBE-GC, we have also made the code publicly available through GitHub, enabling users to download and modify it according to their specific requirements. In the process of developing OpBE-GC, several important research questions arose that require further investigation, including the potential benefits of integrating OpBE-GC with other efficient algorithms and the potential for developing more advanced algorithms based on the BE framework. We employ numerical simulations to generate two types of jamming models under discrete time evolution: frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming. Our findings reveal that the former exhibits characteristic behaviors of frictionless isotropic jamming, including power law relationships between stress and distance from jamming, as well as a distinct plateau in the frictionless isotropic jamming scenario. Conversely, the latter exhibits distinct exponents compared to frictionless isotropic jamming, yet shares common power law characteristics with frictional shear jamming generated through quasi-static means. Additionally, we discover that the latter model's stress-to-kT ratio decreases with increasing temperature, and that its thermal expansion coefficient equals zero, in contrast to the former model's coefficient equaling one-tenth. Furthermore, we observe that the latter model's power law exponent $\nu$ equals two-dimensional space's target value of $1.5$, when undergoing shear jamming. Our research provides tangible evidence for two distinct jamming states with distinct properties, and suggests that the term "jamming transition" is actually a transition between two different jamming states rather than a continuous process. We propose renaming this transition the "shear jamming transition". Our results also reveal a discontinuous relationship between stress and distance from jamming, in addition to power law relationships between other relevant physical quantities, and predict the target exponent $\nu$ for two-dimensional shear jamming to be $1.5$. Our simulations also demonstrate the necessity of using frictionless isotropic jamming as a reference point for the comparison of other jamming states' exponents. We propose that the term "jamming transition" be replaced with "shear jamming transition" to better reflect our findings. The paired-permutation test, also known as the paired-randomization test, is an exact statistical method used to compare the means of paired samples. This test requires calculating all possible permutations of data, which becomes computationally expensive as the number of data points increases. We have developed a new algorithm to efficiently perform this test, reducing the necessary calculations from O(n!) to O(n^2) for a single permutation of n data points, achieving this decrease through the use of our new efficient permutation generation method. We have further observed that using Monte Carlo approximation results in significantly longer computation time than the new exact algorithm. When comparing the new algorithm to existing exact methods that use inverse permutation to find matching data, we found that these methods are actually implementing the pairwise permutation test for two samples, not paired samples. We have also modified the new algorithm to match the pair-testing scenario, finding that the paired-permutation test is equivalent to pairing two randomization tests together. We have further developed this concept to create a more efficient algorithm for the two-sample permutation test, also known as the two-sample randomization test. This test is commonly used in the analysis of running times in algorithms. We have also applied the paired-permutation test to the analysis of cache-oblivious algorithms. We have further developed a method to pair the upper and lower bound running times together, achieving the pair through the use of an auxiliary data structure known as an balance diagram. We have also determined the paired running time bound for several cache-oblivious algorithms, including sort, link, and priority queue algorithms. We have also established a method to pair the upper and lower bound running times for tree-based algorithms, achieving this pairing through the use of balance diagrams based on tree height and sort order. The shipping industry is known for its strong competition and fragmented nature, but it has historically been characterized by competitive pricing through shipping cartels. These cartels controlled not only freight rates but also shipping quantities, causing concerns among regulators about their anti-competitive effects. In 1993, Japan eliminated its shipping cartel laws, leading to a significant increase in freight rates and a decrease in shipping quantities for several years after the change. This paper uses new data on shipping quantities and prices to refine the previous understanding of how cartels respond to deregulation, revealing a more complex dynamic where freight rates and shipping quantities fluctuated in the short and long term. Moreover, freight rates were found to have increased more substantially in the year following the ban, while shipping quantities took longer to respond, increasing by 20% in the long term. Furthermore, the research discovered that the shipping industry's ability to adapt to changes in demand and supply was impaired by the absence of cartels, leading to freight rate and shipping quantity patterns that differed from those observed during the cartel era. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the shipping industry requires stronger incentives to reduce prices and increase shipping quantities, with implications for current antitrust policies. Additionally, the new data and analytical approach provide a basis for evaluating recent shipping industry mergers and acquisitions, like the Nippon Express and NYK Integration, and offer regulators a tool to assess the effectiveness of antitrust laws and industry structure. The research also raises questions about the effectiveness of recent shipping industry antitrust laws and the need for new policies that prioritize consumer interests and shipping quantity aggregation. The FreighQuant data used in this study is available for public use, covering 93% of Japan's ship cargo volume from 1993 to 2018. The dataset includes daily observations of shipping quantities and prices for 21,000 shipping routes worldwide, offering a valuable resource for researchers and industry stakeholders. The study's findings are also applicable to other shipping industries, like those in the United States and Europe, where shipping cartels have been banned for longer periods, allowing for a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics governing the shipping industry. In this paper, a 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization is employed to develop a linearized general relativity theory that allows for the analytical expansion of metric perturbations in the massive particle's field. This expansion involves developing successive approximation methods to calculate the components of the metric tensor at various orders. In the case where the massive particle is confined to its ground state in a harmonic trap, we derive an exact expression for the metric tensor's components as well as the associated energy momentum tensor. Furthermore, we determine the analytical expression for the energy momentum tensor's component associated with the outgoing electromagnetic wave and show that it corresponds to a specific conformally charged Janiszewski plane (CJP) in flat spacetime. The Standard FGMRES (SFGMRES) method has emerged as a powerful algorithm for solving large linear systems in Recent Years. We acknowledge the significant advantages it offers over the conventional GMRES iteration, particularly in exploiting sparse matrices and sparsifiable residual vectors. However, in certain situations where the precision requires a smaller number of iterations, the SFGMRES method may fail to deliver improved results. This paper introduces an enhanced version of the standard FGMRES iteration, namely the Modified SFGMRES (MSGMRES) method, which is designed to overcome the limitations of its predecessor by introducing a new starting point for the iteration that is more effective in achieving a smaller number of iterations with lower precision. We provide a theoretical analysis of the message complexity of the MSGMRES method, comparing it favourably with the SFGMRES method, and demonstrate the proposed algorithm's efficacy through numerical experiments presented in the results section. Additionally, the MSGMRES method has been implemented in the open-source matrix-free solver, NGSolve, with the accompanying examples shown in the additional file part. This new algorithm offers significant advantages over existing methods and is particularly well-suited for solving various PDE-based systems, including the Stokes problem, the Cahn-Hilliard equation, the MHD sheldon model, the nonlinear elasticity problem, the minimal surface problem, and the pure phase field model. Establishing optical flow between images is a self-supervised problem that yields a robust and versatile representation for subsequent computer vision tasks. Despite the success of contrastive learning methods, there are still significant challenges to overcome, particularly with regard to modeling occlusions. We propose a novel, contrastive learning-based approach called Contrastive Flow Estimation (ConFlow) that utilizes two distinct representations of an image's content to encourage the estimation of accurate optical flow. ConFlow succeeds in learning a representation that facilitates seamless navigation across neighboring points in the data manifold without relying on contrastive learning contrasts. By leveraging our proposed encoder, we demonstrate that only a minimal amount of additional training is required to achieve state-of-the-art results on both the MPII Human Pose and KITTI datasets. Moreover, ConFlow yields notable gains in other vision tasks, including human pose estimation and unsupervised domain adaptation, without incurring substantial computational expenses. Despite its efficacy, we discover that ConFlow is prone to mistakes in areas with significant ocisions, highlighting areas for future research. Our code is available at https://github.com/leovoolevy/ConFlow.

We define the term even-2-factorable (E2F) to describe cubic graphs that have a 2-factor consisting entirely of cycles of even length. We dedicate this special issue to discovering the E2F properties of various classes of cubic graphs, including graph configurations, such as graphs with specified component combinations, graphs featuring specific structural patterns, and random cubic graphs. We address the E2F property predictions for these cubic graph scenarios. Despite the fact that determining whether a cubic graph is E2F is inherently difficult, we have successfully developed three distinct approaches to resolving this question for different types of cubic graphs. These methods involve utilizing a 2-factorization algorithm, a result derived from the strong 3-colorability property, and the use of random graph theory. We discuss the potential applications and theoretical implications of our findings. We have also included two algorithmic sections in this special issue. We have made the 2-factor finding and 2-factorization algorithms associated with the E2F property of cubic graphs publicly available on the website associated with the research project 'CubicGraphs'. User-level system call filtering is crucial for enhancing the security of computer systems.  A majority of system filtering approaches are designed with C-based applications in mind, using Linux's Syscall interface. These systems bypass system call filtering when dealing with applications written in interpreted languages, such as Python and PHP.  To address this limitation, we present Timeloops, a lightweight and secure Linux platform that implements system call filtering for such applications.  Timeloops redirects system calls for each application to a private namespace, where they are mapped from the application's current executable to a precomputed table, ensuring only authorized system calls can be made.  To minimize performance costs, system calls are compiled in advance to their native binary form, eliminating extra decomposition steps during execution.  Our tests show that Timeloops offers significant performance gains over existing system filtering solutions.  Furthermore, Timeloops' simple design makes its source code highly customizable for users and developers seeking to modify its features.  Our research demonstrates how system call filtering can be effectively combined with other security mechanisms, such as memory autoshaping and mandatory access control, to provide a more secure computer system.  The Timeloops platform is designed to be extendable to other interpreted languages and comes with sample implementations for Python, PHP, and JavaScript.  In addition to system call filtering, Timeloops can also be used to enforce application memory constraints, execute application code with reduced privileges, and execute application code in a sandboxed environment.  Our results are available on the Timeloops website, along with the platform's underlying code.  Our research offers a novel approach to enhancing computer system security and presents a practical solution to address the system call filtering challenges faced by applications written in interpreted languages.  Our work demonstrates how system call filtering can be an indispensable component of various computer system security mechanisms, such as memory autoshaping and sandboxing.  Our findings provide valuable insights for users, developers, and researchers seeking to enhance the security of computer systems and applications.  Our research is applicable to a wide range of computer systems and applications, including high-performance computing clusters, web services, and cloud computing platforms. Our team encourages public engagement with our research, inviting feedback and suggestions from the computer science community. The asymmetric noisy voter model is a random process that involves two distinct species interacting within a population, and it can be described as a combination of birth, death, and conversion events. These events are made "noisy" by no longer being certain, with noisy processes no longer producing the expected outcomes. In our research, we explored the competitions between two species that interact in opposite directions, and our findings reveal a wide range of possible eventual outcomes, including the extinction of one species, its replacement by the other, or the coexistence of both species. These possible outcomes are determined by the rates of species interaction, birth, death, and the level of uncertainty. Our noisy model is comparable to the asymmetric voter model, with similar parameters, but it includes an additional mechanism of outcome uncertainty, which can cause opposite outcomes to the asymmetric voter model to arise, such as the extinction of the species that has the higher birth rate in the noisy model. Our research also discovered a unique threshold at which the outcome changes from the extinction of one species to the coexistence of both species, and it can occur suddenly or gradually, depending on the level of uncertainty. Additionally, our findings reveal that the noisy model has an increased tendency to favor the survival of the species with the higher birth rate, which can be attributed to the certain outcomes of birth events, rather than a preference for the species with the opposite direction of interaction, as seen in the asymmetric voter model. Our research also compared the noisy model with the asymmetric simple majority process, which involves three species interacting in a circle, and it shows that the asymmetric simple majority process can result from the noisy voter model, but it requires a specific set of parameters and the presence of a third species. Our findings are accompanied by numerical simulations that confirm our analytical findings, and they involve two and three species in different settings. Our research provides the mathematical equations that define the asymmetric noisy voter model, and it can be used as a foundation for further modifications and extensions of the model. Understanding the intricate processes of retinal development, particularly the movement of nerve cells called nuclei, is crucial for addressing neurological disorders affecting the eyes. In most eye-forming models, incoming nerve cells are found equally distributed across the developing retina, but the underlying mechanisms behind this balanced distribution are not well understood. Our research reveals that a specific pattern of distributed nuclei dynamics in the retina, observed in zebrafish, is controlled by a mathematical rule that reflects the retinal area growth. By applying this rule, we used a computer simulation to replicate the observed dynamics of nerve cell distribution, further validated by comparing it with actual data from the Zebrafish. This study demonstrates how a simple mathematical principle governs the movement of nerve cells during the early stages of retinal development and confirms that the pattern of distributed dynamics is indeed an intrinsic property of the retina itself. This approach uses a combination of forward discretized flows and feedback flows to construct a chain of states that represents the possible outcomes of feedback control over time. As a result, the resulting reachable state set remains contained in a tubular neighborhood of the original trajectory, enabling us to determine the maximum time a system can remain stable based on its current state and parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this method by applying it to a nonlinear, feedback-controlled aircraft system. Our feedback-based reachability analysis algorithm is a critical component of an aircraft's stability prediction system that we have developed, which provides critical information for controlled descent techniques, especially in emergency situations. Finally, our aircraft system serves as a relevant example for the reachability analysis of other highly nonlinear, time-varying systems that exhibit dynamic behavior during flight, which can inform the design of controlled descent strategies for multiple-scenario applications. Furthermore, our verification process includes a precise assessment of the number of quantum computations required to achieve a certain level of accuracy in these algorithms. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a formal verification process that ensures the reliability of programs on a quantum computer. Understanding and measuring the magnetic field on open flares surfaces relies on mapping vector magnetic field components. However, measuring one component is insufficient and can lead to incorrect conclusions about the direction of magnetic field reversal. To accurately determine the direction of magnetic field reversal at flare sites, we must account for the fill fraction of magnetic fields and ensure that the zero-line crossing in mapped vector magnetic field components occurs after taking this fraction into consideration. Failing to do so results in unreliable estimates of magnetic field reversal sites, particularly for weak field areas. Based on calculations and comparisons with actual Sun observations, we find that the 90dB fill fraction threshold, which is commonly observed on solar flares surfaces, can lead to incorrect conclusions about magnetic field reversal sites, particularly in the contexts of X-ray bright grain boundaries and weak field regions. Consequently, we believe that the current standard for setting fill fraction to zero may contribute to the limited success of magnetseismology techniques that rely on accurate analysis of solar flares surfaces. We also propose possible improvements to achieving more accurate magnetic field assessments.

We then establish the Coxeter group's volume formula as the product of the wedge's volume and the number of spheres in the wedge, raised to a power equal to half the dimension of the vector space. By dimension, we mean the minimum number at which the vector space's dimension exceeds by 1 a significant parameter in its original representation. A key factor in this formula is the topological property of the Fermi surface, captured through the use of a topological quantity called the Fermi surface index. This index can be determined from the known quantities of the material's composition, crystal structure, and positioning of the Fermi level. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this formula, calculations were performed for 12 transition metal alloys with a high sensitivity to magnetic field, and the results showed that the magnetic susceptibility is directly proportional to the square of the spin orbit coupling and the square of the electron density at the Fermi level. Notably, these proportions hold true even in nickel, a metal with a disordered Fermi surface that is considered a key reference point in the field. Interestingly, the minimal change in the topological property of the Fermi surface in nickel suggests that this property is relatively stable in the presence of strong coupling and electron pairing, and that the magnetic susceptibility in this material can be primarily attributed to the spin orbit coupling rather than the electron pairing. Additionally, a comparison was made between the experimental and calculated values of the magnetic susceptibility in nickel, with a very small difference of 1.5 x 10^-5 emu/mol between them. Finally, a discussion is presented on the relationship between the topological property of the Fermi surface and the spin orbit coupling in metal alloys, along with the potential applications of this property in the development of new materials with unique magnetic properties. The equilibrium properties of a system in constant pressure, where the variable pressure serves as a constraint, are examined to determine the conditions under which the grand canonical ensemble is statistically representative.  A crucial assessment is made of the compressibility of the system to establish the validity of the grand canonical ensemble.  In general, a minimum requirement of small adiabatic compressibility is established as necessary for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble.  A critical analysis is performed of the adiabatic compression criterion in relation to the ideal gas model and Polytropic fluid models.  In both cases, precise criteria are derived to determine the validity of the grand canonical ensemble.  In addition, the investigation involves the evaluation of the condition of constant entropy as a criterion for its validity.  A critical evaluation is performed of this condition in both the ideal gas and Polytropic fluid scenarios.  A important conclusion can be drawn from the investigation: the condition of constant entropy is more stringent than the requirement of constant temperature and serves as a necessary condition for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble.  The investigation also involves the examination of the mean square fluctuation of particle number in relation to the mean square displacement in random compressional processes. If-then relation if may state that "if it rains, then the road will be wet". This type of statement contains an if-part (antecedent), a then-part (consequence), and is considered a cause-effect relationship. We argue that training neural models on the structure of these if-then relationships, including their sub-types such as contrast, consequence, cause-effect, and condition, can benefit their performance on classification tasks. Our investigation involves introducing a new multi-task learning framework that combines classification with prediction of if-then relationship types. We select the SubSense dataset, which incorporates if-then relationship labels into sentence semantics, to conduct our experiments. On this dataset, a model trained on both classification and relation prediction tasks for cause-effect relationships shows improved performance compared to models trained on the classification task alone. Additionally, our analysis reveals that neural models struggle to identify cause-effect relationships, suggesting that they are difficult even for modern models. Our findings also indicate that models can be induced to recognize these relationships by introducing a binary cause-effect relation label, showing that our approach is feasible. Our framework and methodology provide a foundation for exploring the incorporation of structural knowledge into neural models in classification tasks involving complex semantic structures. We anticipate that our work will be building on it in the future. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuyonghu/MTL_CSE.

In response, we've developed the NISQ-HHL algorithm, a modified version of HHL tailored for quantum devices, enabling the efficient approximation of matrix inverses and allowing for the efficient execution of various HHL variants. Leveraging phase estimation via Hamiltonian simulation, NISQ-HHL circumvents the quantum inverse transformation and tackles challenges like quantum noise and limited quantum bit counts. We've also developed a novel technique, quantum inverse transformation via Hamiltonian simulation, that serves as a key component for approximate matrix inversion. On top of this, we've crafted a novel QISIGN-style optimization method, known as QISIGN-E, which, in conjunction with NISQ-HHL, enables the efficient solution of linear systems by approximation. To illustrate the practical applications of NISQ-HHL, we've developed a sample code executing Gaussian process regression on a quantum device. Moreover, we've created QISIGN-E and NISQ-HHL modules, along with documentation and examples, to facilitate the integration of these algorithms into existing quantum simulation frameworks. Although NISQ-HHL comes with an enhanced quantum cost, it also offers the benefit of being relatively insensitive to quantum noise, making it a promising option for executing HHL-like tasks on mature quantum hardware. In the course of this research, several novel quantum algorithms were discovered, including a quantum version of Anderson's mixed Poisson process, which can be utilized for, among other things, the efficient simulation of qiBitRAM, a recently introduced random bit generation method. To enhance the association between speech features and linguistic details in deep automated speech recognition systems, a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) is introduced, consisting of a forward attention network that connects speech encodings and linguistic representations, and a reverse attention network that connects the result of the forward attention computation to the speech features. Initially, BiAM is integrated with a conventional sequence-to-sequence model, following which attention defects were observed in the forward network. To rectify this attention defect, the forward attention map is modified to represent the relevance of speech features to linguistic context by averaging the attention weights with the speech encodings. Named BiAM-A, this variation removes attention defects and facilitates the inference of linguistic structures from speech. Named BiAM-W, a variation with the reverse attention map generated from the averaged speech encodings facilitates the inference of speech features from linguistic structure. BiAM-A and BiAM-W are combined to form a unified model which yields superior results on the Switchboard and Church datasets. Furthermore, both BiAM-A and BiAM-W are found to be superior to the baseline sequence-to-sequence model on the English conversational dialogue transcription task, in both 500-word and long-distance scenarios. Additionally, both models are found to be noise-resistant and converge faster than the baseline model in cross-domain speech recognition tasks. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that BiAM can adapt to various architectures and task settings, thereby providing a versatile attention mechanism for automated speech recognition systems. Experimental outcomes also indicate that BiAM is adept at capturing long-distance dependencies in speech inputs, outperforming lattice-based and n-gram-based approaches in several scenarios. Ultimately, the attention weights and the learned hidden states from BiAM-A and BiAM-W can be utilized as features for zero-shot learning, as demonstrated by the transmission of linguistic structures to novel domains and tasks. Word embeddings learned through BiAM-A and BiAM-W also exhibit improved performance in tumor classification and cancer prognosis, indicating the utility of these embeddings in various machine learning tasks. The attention weights and the learned hidden states from BiAM-A and BiAM-W are publicly available at https://github.com/QingyuXu/BiAM-Embeddings. A propagating instability of the supercurrent has been uncovered in nanowire Josephson junctions under DC bias, allowing the threshold voltage for this instability to be controlled and placed anywhere within the junction's voltage range. To observe this phenomenon, a setup was developed to quickly change the starting voltage for a nanowire Josephson circuit while listening to the resulting sound, both literally and figuratively. Once an appropriate beginning voltage is found, the circuit can be stabilized, and a stable, large-amplitude current can be maintained for an extended period, potentially finding utility in applications like nanoscale radio transmitters. The mechanism behind this stability or instability can be understood by considering the shape of the Josephson current double hump. Notably, this phenomenon was observed in nanowires made from W, Ti, and Niobium, but not in bulk Josephson junctions. The condition for this stability or instability can also be described in terms of the energy of the involved photons, offering a possible pathway to its utilization in quantum simulators. The versatility of this phenomenon has been demonstrated by modifying the starting voltage, the width of the Josephson current peak, the energy of the involved photons, the wire length, and the material of the wire itself. The study has also revealed that this instability can result in a negative differential resistance, potentially facilitating simple wire-based oscillators that require no additional components. The most straightforward configuration of such an oscillator has been tested and found to be functional, suggesting that supercurrent instabilities could be valuable in the development of nanoscale transmitters and receivers in quantum computing and other applications. The research has been conducted using W nanowire Josephson junctions, offering promising results that are likely applicable to a broader range of materials. The study has been performed in a cryogenic environment using a superconducting quantum circuit, and the findings have been analyzed through both experimental data and theoretical models. The discovery of this propagating instability has been observed in about 30% of nanowire Josephson junctions, and the condition for its occurrence can be adjusted to place the threshold voltage anywhere within the junction's voltage range. As WiFi fingerprint-based positioning systems become more widespread, the need to accurately estimate distance between geospatial locations has increased. Typically, this distance is estimated through kernel approximation methods like the Nearest Neighbor Distance Distribution (NNDD). While NNDD proves effective for this purpose, it requires a considerable amount of data to function smoothly. This issue is particularly pronounced in applications where location measurements are limited, leading to poorly estimated distances. A novel approach called Graph Convolution Distance Distribution (GCDD) is presented to enhance the estimation of geospatial distance using WiFi fingerprints. GCDD frames the distance estimation problem as a graph-based learning task, utilizing sparse information more efficiently. Through convolution neural networks, it leverages global information to address the limited data challenge, resulting in GCDD. This model can be used in conjunction with various kernel distance measures, including NNDD. Through extensive simulations based on real-world data sets, GCDD demonstrates its superiority over existing methods, leading to several potential applications in the field of WiFi fingerprinting. These include location tracking, community detection, and geographic route optimization. Moreover, due to its model-independent nature, GCDD can be applied to other learning tasks involving graph representations of data. Code for GCDD is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chenyue0327/GCDD_WifiFingerprinting. Next, a more comprehensive GCDD-based framework is introduced to support the ongoing measurement process and the associated geographic mapping, making it suitable for real-time location tracking and mapping in sparsely connected scenarios, as shown in the accompanying paper titled Convolution Neural Networks for Efficient Geospatial Mapping with Temporally Separated WiFi Data. Notably, the code for GCDD and the accompanying framework is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/Chenyue0327/GCDD_WifiFingerprinting. The impact of model size on GCDD's performance was investigated by experimenting with different number of layers in the convolution neural network, revealing a direct correlation between the two. Consequently, an efficient model was developed for GCDD, resulting in a notable reduction in model size without a decline in accuracy. The resulting GCDD model comprises 175,507 parameters, achieving the optimal balance between size and accuracy, and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chenyue0327/GCDD_WifiFingerprinting. The GCDD-based framework was validated through multiple simulations based on real-world datasets, showing its effectiveness in mapping and tracking locations with WiFi connectivity. We analyze the impact of a simple uniform filling pattern where equal charges are placed in each bunch, affecting the threshold current in a negative way. Additionally, varying the uniform filling pattern's value can impact the stability of radiofrequency (RF) fields, influencing the choice of suitable filling patterns. Our study utilizes a single-bunch model, considering the influence of uniform fill patterns on threshold current and RF field stability, offering a basic framework for more complex applications. We define a new metric, the over-voltage factor, which compares the uniform fill pattern's value to the ideal value, providing a straightforward way to evaluate the influence of fill patterns on RF field stability. We further investigate how this metric changes along the linac when considering a two-pass scenario. Our study provides a starting point for more sophisticated models, especially those incorporating multiple bunch filling patterns in multi-pass ERLs. We also introduce the concept of the effective fill pattern, obtained by combining the fill patterns of entrance and exit beams, which significantly affects the threshold current and RF field stability in multi-pass ERLs. Our research demonstrates a straightforward approach to calculating the effective fill pattern, along with associated metrics, by using data from experiments already in operation. We believe our study is crucial for optimizing beam-RF interactions in multi-pass ERLs, especially those using the uniform filling pattern, which needs to be addressed urgently due to the growing number of such facilities worldwide. Our work is essential for facilities like the ICRF-based 1.3 GeV SARAF accelerator in Israel. We anticipate our findings being useful for other similar machines, such as the 500 MeV ERL test facility at the High Power Research Institute in China. The metric dimension of (V, E) with this distance function is denoted as β(G). It has been proven that for any graph with this distance function, there exists a integer threshold t_0 = 2√|V| - 1 below which the metric dimension is 1. A more significant contribution from this research reveals that for any graph with this distance function, there exists a integer threshold t_1 = |V| - √|V| + 1 above which the metric dimension is |V| - 1. Additionally, several classes of graphs, including random graphs, regular graphs, and trees, have their corresponding threshold values provided. Furthermore, the concept of geodesic distance tractance can be applied to undirected and weighted graphs, proven by showing that the original graph and its weighted version have the same metric dimension. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly across broad energy spectra, and long observational periods are needed to fully understand their behavior. However, traditional analysis approaches are often hindered by data inconsistencies and different observation lengths, which can affect the accuracy of conclusions drawn from them. In this study, we analyzed the (U)UV variability of the quasar SF9 using extensive data from the Hubble Space Telescope, totaling around 30 years and consisting of multiple observations with varying intervals between them. We initially investigated the variability of this quasar at a single epoch through correlation spectrum mapping, but further examination revealed issues with internal consistency and varying observation intervals, which can cause significant errors in conclusions drawn from them. Therefore, we adjusted the analysis to account for these challenges, incorporating observations with intervals of up to 13 years and 32 observations of (U)UV light, and ensuring that all data points were reliably aligned. We further investigated the variability patterns of SF9, comparing its behavior to four coronal models, and exploring the limitations of current coronal model simulations in predicting the variability of AGNs over extended periods.

Recently, researchers introduced the concept of valuation functions based on bipartite matchings and directed graphs to approximate the social welfare in various scenarios. Later, it was shown that using these valuations could result in a 1 approximated social welfare in both single and multi-agent settings. However, these previous studies suggested that the approximation quality could be enhanced with additional information. Due to the large number of small asteroids detected in wide-field surveys, 3D shape reconstruction and spin orbit alignment determination have become challenging tasks. Binary asteroid candidates are often missed in detailed examinations because the statistical methods used to identify them are not effective in discovering small particle orbits. A different approach is needed that utilizes the characteristics of images to help reveal hidden structures. A solution to this challenge is provided by point spread function analysis techniques, normally used in optical engineering and image processing, which can offer valuable information about an asteroid's spin, mass, and close-around satellites. Research is presented on utilizing three methods of point spread function analysis (minimum description length, regularized maximum likelihood, and artificial neural networks) to apply a simple model to surveys featuring wide-field views of large fields, including Pan-STARRS and the Dark Energy Camera. Detailed examples of fitting point spread functions to images of single asteroids are given, along with a binary asteroid population synthesis model used for comparison with observed patterns. Although many surveyed asteroids are too large for a perturbed orbit model, the research demonstrates that small mass ratios ($\lesssim 0.01$) can still be detected with good accuracy. A threshold is proposed for detecting small mass ratios based on the blurring of the asteroid's shape, and a statistical analysis is provided for binary asteroid candidates found in surveys featuring targeted observations of specific fields, including the All-Sky Survey and the Pan-STARRS intermediate data release. A binary asteroid candidate detection method is also introduced that takes into account both mass ratios and the minimum orbiting period, and the research estimates the fraction of binary asteroids as a function of mass, which is found to be 0.44 $pm 0.17$ for a size range of 100 km to 300 km. A model is then used to estimate the number of binary asteroids yet to be discovered in the population of small asteroids found in future surveys featuring wide-field views of large fields, including the Lucid Camera Survey and the Pan-STARRS survey with a proposed second generation. A discussion is also presented on the limitations of spin orbit alignment determination and potential solutions. The research concludes by presenting a binary asteroid population as a potential component of small asteroid populations in the solar system, and by highlighting the potential of future surveys featuring wide-field views of large fields for discovering the complex structures within small asteroids. The research's findings, models, and examples can be applied to future surveys featuring targeted observations of specific fields, including the All-Sky Survey and the Pan-STARRS intermediate data release

We present an original approach to assess network effects resulting from interactions within a system of connections, taking into account both direct and indirect relationships. This methodological innovation enables the estimation of influential nodes and provides insights into network dynamics by considering the comprehensive structure of connections. We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of this approach by applying it to a policy-relevant question, namely, evaluating the impact of a federal research funding program on collaboration among academics. We show that this approach yields accurate and efficient results, surpassing those of alternative methods, and reveals compelling evidence on the causal effects of connections on academic collaboration. Furthermore, we find that funding enhances the influence of notable researchers who, in turn, are more likely to connect with their peers, leading to a surge in published papers and citations. Nonetheless, we discover that fedf funding may result in a redistribution of research influence from non-funded to funded academics, with a more significant shift observed among academics from institutions that are not primary funders. We also observe a citation advantage from receiving grants, particularly those considered highly influential, and that these citations are largely directed toward previously published work. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the value of considering the complex structure of connections and relationships when examining policy interventions and network dynamics. We also contribute to the existing literature on academic collaboration by providing a detailed analysis of connection formation and citation outcomes in the context of research collaboration. This research paper develops multiple chain rule formulas for variable-order fractional operators in several dimensions. It begins by introducing the operator's definition and then derives differentiable chain rule formulas for both the partial derivative and gradient operators. Furthermore, it demonstrates the equivalence of these operators to the Laplace operator, leading to the development of the Laplace operator's chain rule formula. Additionally, the paper establishes relationships between the variable-order fractional operator and the Laplace operator, enabling it to extend existing theorems about the Laplace operator. Finally, it provides some examples highlighting the applicability of these chain rule formulas to variable-order fractional partial differential equations.

We presented a novel collaborative game framework called MindWiki, which incorporates theory-of-mind (ToM) capabilities in agents to enhance goal attainment. By integrating ToM, the game provides agents with mental state information about Wikipedia content, reducing the need for extensive web searches. We modified the standard MultiWiki game to prioritize ToM integration and provided an improved version with Wikipedia content, accompanying benchmarks and detailed methodology for future ToM games. Our data shows that the MindWiki game outperforms the baseline (Mean: 10.5) in terms of goal achievement (Mean: 15.1) and requires significantly less search time (Baseline: 13.4 minutes, MindWiki: 1.8 minutes). Furthermore, an interview with game experts revealed positive feedback on the game's integrity and engaging nature, suggesting MindWiki's potential as a viable ToM game. Moreover, the framework and associated data can be utilized as benchmarks for future ToM games and related research. MindWiki, alongside its accompanying dataset, is available at https://mindwiki.cs.columbia.edu/. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation Grant IIS-2046019. Our research proposes the DISCO approach to counterfactual generation, which
allows for the creation of counterfactual data to train machine learning models
on. Counterfactual data consists of observations from a hypothetical
alternativeworld, different from the one we live in, yet sharing many similar
characteristics. When incorporated into models, this type of data can enhance
their ability to generalize and be more robust. To develop the DISCO framework,
we drew upon counterfactual theory as well as insights from econometrics and
artificial intelligence. Our research involves designing an algorithm to
counterfactually alter features of data, developing a metric to measure the
counterfactual distance between datasets, and creating a method to generate
counterfactual data on multiple unseen datasets. Through computational experiments, we found that training models on counterfactual data made using the DISCO framework improves their robustness and ability to generalize, leading to models that perform better on novel datasets than models trained on real data alone. Moreover, our research reveals that the counterfactual distance metric plays a significant role in determining the quality of the generated counterfactual data, thereby influencing the performance of models trained on it. In addition, we discovered that the DISCO algorithm can effectively produce counterfactual datasets that exist in real-world settings, such as in relationships between variables that follow specific patterns, by deliberately altering particular aspects of existing datasets. To demonstrate the practical applications of the DISCO framework, we created a demonstration website that allows for the counterfactual generation of various real-world datasets, including those related to economics and machine learning, and makes the associated code available on GitHub. Furthermore, we developed a counterfactual data pipeline for training machine learning models on robust and generalized models using an open-source framework, and made this pipeline available on GitHub as well. With the DISCO framework and associated materials available to the public, we hope to stimulate further research and development in the field of counterfactual generation, as well as encourage widespread adoption in real-world settings. Our research paper has been well-received, with our research being highlighted in the top 10% most cited papers at the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning according to the conference's website. Our research also won the best paper award at the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning. Our research has several practical implications for various fields of work. In the field of economics, our research can be applied to counterfactually generate data that enables policy-makers to evaluate the impact of specific policies on economic variables.

Researchers who use graphene as a growth substrate for epitaxial materials often encounter a problem where different areas of the sample grow distinct material structures due to varying temperatures. This issue hinders consistent material production and prevents realization of two-dimensional heterostructures. This study demonstrates that growing a thin layer of aluminum oxide on graphene prior to epitaxial material growth can prevent temperature-induced domain structures and ensure consistent material growth at high temperatures. It also reveals that the crystalline quality of graphene significantly impacts the success of this approach. By using high-quality graphene, researchers can realize uniform material structures on large scales, meeting the strict standards for two-dimensional heterostructure devices. Moreover, by optimizing growth conditions, researchers can remove impurities and ensure uniform material compositions across the entire sample. This approach has been successfully applied to automate growth of sic and hbn layers on large areas (up to 10 mm^2) and 300mm Si wafers. This study paves the way for the production of two-dimensional heterostructures with atomic precision and scalability. This discovery can be extended to growth substrates other than graphene and provides a robust solution for addressing the domain structure problem in silicon and other materials. This approach has been validated by modeling and simulated with ab initio calculations, which reveal that layer-by-layer transition metal oxides can prevent domain structures by increasing the energy barrier for nucleation and allowing consistent material growth at high temperatures. This approach has the potential to revolutionize the production of two-dimensional materials and heterostructures by addressing a critical issue that has long hindered the development of silicon and other materials. This study offers a viable solution for this problem and provides valuable insights into the physical principles underlying it. This knowledge can be utilized to develop more efficient and scalable methods for producing two-dimensional materials and heterostructures with atomic precision. Building on the ideas presented in a paper by Cigona and Gluck, we explore the connection between weakly natural transformations and adjoint functors, investigating conditions under which a weakly natural transformation can be classified as part of an adjunction. We establish a more general framework for this relationship, one that is independent of specific categorical settings, and discover it is driven by the properties of identities and composition within the category. In addition, we provide a theoretical model that serves as a foundation for future categorical constructions in this domain. Furthermore, we examine the case of immersions and biadjoint functors, establishing a categorical relationship that mirrors the concept of biadjointness. Lastly, we demonstrate applications of these ideas to the category of distributive lattices and modular lattices, showing that a specific transformation is not part of an adjunction, a result with implications for the theory of continuous functions. In this process, we uncover a subcategory of the latter lattice family that escapes this non-adjoint transformation, providing a novel achievement within the field of formal concept lattices. The conventional approach to analyzing these signals involves isolating cardiac activity, but our proposed method extracts distinctive patterns from the original signals to facilitate accurate classification. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, as our network achieves a 20% higher accuracy rate compared to existing methods for classification of epileptic seizures and an additional 10% accuracy gain for classification of cardiac arrhythmias, on datasets with ambulatory EEG signals contaminated by artificially generated noise. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits robust performance across various noise levels, as evidenced by significant improvements (25% to 50%) in classification performance when comparing noisy to noiseless data. This comes at a computational cost, as our method requires approximately twice the amount of data needed for conventional deep networks to achieve the same accuracy level. Nonetheless, this proposed method presents a promising solution for the detection of cardiac abnormalities in real-world applications. The efficiency of an interview panel can be significantly enhanced through the systematic deployment of a scoring system, which prioritizes the most effective panel members for each interview. This study aims to introduce a concept of value evaluation, enabling the comparison of panel values, and develop an algorithm to maximize value additions during recruitment interviews. A graphical explanation for the scoring strategy is provided, along with a binary action tree optimization through depth-first search. The study also presents two variants of the panel generation problem: open, where interviews are conducted in sequence, and closed, where interviews are conducted in a fixed set of sessions. For the open problem, a greedy algorithm is proposed, and for the closed problem, an algorithm leveraging recursive descent is proposed. The efficacy of these algorithms is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world data. The study's findings reveal a notable improvement in panel efficiency following the implementation of a scoring system and the successful execution of algorithms on sizable datasets. The proposed approaches have the added benefit of ensuring that the best panel members are retained for future reference, should the need arise. The study's results highlight the potential advantages of algorithmic strategies in recruitment practices despite the existing alternatives being relatively simple. The most efficient algorithm identified demonstrated a near-linear performance, demonstrating its suitability for a broad range of applications. The study's findings are expected to enhance the understanding of intuitive scoring systems and efficient panel generation through algorithmic means. The proposed approach can be applied to a broader context of ranking and selecting the most suitable items from a larger pool, making it a relevant contribution to this domain as well. The study's data and software are available for public access, and the proposed algorithms can be used as part of potential future work, such as combining them with genetic algorithms or other nature-inspired strategies. The recruitment panel generation problem has been found to exhibit a high degree of complexity, making it a challenging and engaging example of an NP-hard problem. The presence of an effective scoring system was found to lead to an increase in panel efficiency, with the magnitude of this increase being directly proportional to the system's fairness level. The study's findings have been demonstrated to be visually intuitive through the use of binary action trees, providing a clear and understandable explanation of the underlying mechanisms. The use of algorithmic approaches was found to result in a significant reduction in panel generation time, with the largest decrease observed in the closed problem case. This research investigates an extended backward stochastic differential equation (BSEDD) that accounts for a underlying diffusion, denoted as the reference BSEDD, and provides a theoretical framework for understanding the optimal payoff in this setting. By demonstrating the uniqueness of solutions to the extended BSEDD and establishing a connection with the reference BSEDD, we are able to apply this relationship to optimize payoff in the underlying diffusion framework. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal payoff in the underlying diffusion setting is equivalent to solving a modified reference BSEDD with an added drift component, which can be interpreted as solving an extended reference BSEDD with a fixed final value. This interpretation enables us to tackle problems with time-dependent obstacles and time-dependent targets by transforming these problems into a fixed-final-value obstacle problem and a fixed-initial-value target problem, respectively. Finally, we illustrate the viability of this approach by applying it to a scenario with a time-dependent target and demonstrate that this target can be reached with the optimal payoff. This research on the optimal payoff with underlying diffusion also incorporates an obstacle problem with a time-dependent barrier, which was previously an independently published result. This research has been accepted for publication in Numerous Advances in Stochastic Differential Equations. The asymmetric production of leptoquark pairs in an electron-proton or a positron-proton collider has been overlooked in previous research. However, this process is feasible in the LHeC and future lepton-hadron colliders, offering promising insights into the properties of leptoquarks, particularly for heavy leptoquarks beyond the top quark. As our primary contribution, we detail the leptoquark pair production processes in these colliders, derive the relevant cross-section equations, and analyze them in the "ajoint" scenario, where we assume that only one type of leptoquark flavor participates in the interaction. As our second contribution, we establish relationships between the leptoquark pair production cross-section and the leptoquark decay into a gauge boson and a neutrino, and we also investigate the impact of the leptoquark mass, the collider energy, and the incoming particle on the cross-section. As our third contribution, we provide usable numerical data for the cross-section at the LHeC, the 50 TeV electron-proton collider, and the 14 TeV LHC with proton beams, and we offer recommendations on necessary leptoquark properties for detection in these colliders. As our fourth contribution, we propose an analytical formula for evaluating the relevant cross-section in the case where only one leptoquark flavor is produced, which can be utilized in the optimal selection of leptoquark masses in future lepton-hadron colliders. As our fifth contribution, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the top-hadron and vector leptoquark modes in the standard model and its $\mathcal{N}=1$ extension, and we also investigate the impact of the colliner and scalar leptoquark modes in the standard model and its $\mathcal{N}=1$ extension on the cross-section. As our sixth contribution, we propose viable detection strategies for leptoquarks in the mass range extending beyond the top quark, and we also outline the necessary improvements required for the next-generation lepton-hadron colliders. The 10.5-meter GALEX ultraviolet telescope and radio telescopes like VLA and LMT were used to analyze three extremely starbursting galaxies with a theoretical power of ten to twenty times that of typical galaxies with such activity. A significant finding in these galaxies was a massive, low-density gas reservoir with a high energy density, likely explaining their extremely active formation of stars. A comparison was also drawn with the Milky Way, revealing that its gas reservoir with similar characteristics covers only one percent of its total size. A highly sensitive technique known as giant pulse phase-switching allowed astronomers to detect neutral gas through the 21-cm wavelength, revealing the detailed structure and movement of these galaxies. Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in PTA experiments involving the combination of multiple pulsar probes. We evaluated three distinct approaches: a detailed numerical simulation-based method, a precise semi-analytic method, and approximate analytic models. The approximate analytic models were developed by two different researchers using different techniques, yet both sourced fundamental components, specifically the individual SNRs for each pulsar and their correlated variations. Through comparative assessments, we found the approximations to be accurate relative to the semi-analytic method, with deviations of 0.09 and 0.09 for the two separate analyses, corresponding to approximately 0.01 units of standard deviation in SNR. Although these deviations are minimal, we highlight the potential risks of using integrated noise models in the context of PTA experiments, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying assumptions and precise calculations, particularly if the research involves the development of PTA data analysis techniques for new pulsar discoveries. Furthermore, we provide a practical example demonstrating the advantages of combined searches that incorporate multi-pulsar observations, and highlight the accessibility of our code online. This code package, in addition to demonstrating the benefits of combined searches, allows for the reproduction of our results and serves as a foundation for future developments of PTA analysis methods. Given the modular design, the code can be utilized for various pulsar-related experiments, including those involving pulsar timing residuals and the evaluation of injection and simulation pulsar models. This work is part of our broader research efforts in pulsar science, particularly in the context of PTA experiments, and reflects our commitment to making our code publicly available to facilitate the development of new PTA analysis techniques and ensure the integrity of future research, should the original data become inaccessible in the future. This research examines the ASEP system to investigate the statistics of a third class of particles that can travel at various speeds, specifically focusing on a system with only two speeds, as time progresses. To better understand the behavior of these third class particles, we establish a corresponding discrete nonlinear interval map, known as the RGH map, and reveal its connection to the statistics of the third class particles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the velocity distribution of these particles adheres to a power law, accumulated at the point of 1, and we utilize the RGH map to explain this distribution. Additionally, we investigate a variant of the ASEP system with two speeds and different initial conditions. In this version, the statistics of the third class particles remain unchanged, while the RGH map exhibits a periodic phase with an extensive duration. Consequently, the power law distribution persists even in this variant. In both systems studied, the power law distribution persists due to the presence of a specific phase of the RGH map that exhibits periodic vast duration. Moreover, we demonstrate that the power law distribution can be expressed in a simplified form by introducing a new parameter known as the distance from the start of the periodic phase. This new parameter demonstrates periodic characteristics over time, and we calculate the associated area under its curve. Finally, we discuss the connection between this power law distribution and other similar power law distributions observed in other systems, suggesting a common underlying cause. This research provides a new perspective on the power law distribution observed in the ASEP system and reveals a connection to a discrete nonlinear interval map. By utilizing the tools of nonlinear dynamics to analyze this power law distribution, we demonstrate the presence of a prolonged periodic phase that gives rise to this distribution, and we investigate the associated parameters and their relationships. This study also establishes a link between the power law distribution and other similar distributions observed in other systems, suggesting a common cause.
