Offline learning for offline multiple agent systems involves using historical data without self-modifying the environment. A significant challenge in this context is agents sharing similar learning trajectories, which slows down learning for new agents. The Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework was recently introduced to address this issue by assuming that agents following the same policy will generate similar data. Building on this assumption, we propose a novel offline multi-agent learning method known as Democratic Maximum Likelihood (DML). In DML, hidden states are predicted using a model that estimates shared trajectories, and an maximum likelihood estimator determines the optimal hidden state prediction model. By incorporating an agent-specific model and shared model in an augmented architecture, DML improves on existing methods by facilitating fast learning for new agents and preserving existing knowledge. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the effectiveness of DML. Additionally, we observe that DML successfully learns from data featuring a wide range of time horizons, including those significantly longer than typical offline learning contexts. The code for DML is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenyuXie/DML.

Deep learning methods, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have been effective in a variety of medical image analysis tasks and can serve as alternatives to traditional algorithm-based solutions. Recently, CNNs have been successful in co-registering medical images by simply feeding paired images into a network and obtaining a deformation field as output. Although this approach yields better results for certain image sets compared to conventional methods, it has been observed to perform inconsistently for other images, often producing suboptimal results. We believe this inconsistency arises from the lack of theoretical foundations underlying CNNs, as they do not guarantee optimal solutions for the problem of finding deformation fields that minimize the distance between original and transformed images. In response to this limitation, we drew inspiration from the CNN architecture to design a straightforward, deep learning-inspired solution for a larger problem space, ultimately leading to a novel algorithm we call the Deep Learning Distance Method (DLDM). This new approach was tested on real-world data and compared to established methods, revealing significant performance enhancements of approximately 3-fold in terms of computational time required to achieve the same level of image quality. In addition to this empirical advantages, DLDM also offers certain theoretical benefits, including the minimalization of the target function it employs. In summary, our proposed method, DLDM, is a computationally efficient, theoretically well-founded solution for medical image registration, showcasing superior performance in co-registering CT images modified by a contrast agent. This research is significant because it contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between the distance measures employed in image registration and those used in deep learning, facilitating potential applications in registering other types of multi-phase images. This work is an extension of our previous research presented at the IEEE International Conference on Image Processing 2023. We investigate the connection between single-particle entanglement, nonlocal effects, and quantum steering in three-qubit Heisenberg XY chain systems. Using the reduced state approach, we first examine single-particle entanglement, quantifying it through the concurrence relative to the full system's entanglement. To facilitate large-scale testing in text-based games, text game simulations typically require significant computation time. Our newly devised framework, TextWorldExpress, accelerates these simulations by reducing the necessary steps to achieve the same outcomes by an average of 24.8 times, according to benchmark tests involving existing text game benchmarks. TextWorldExpress achieves this performance improvement by a different strategy than previous fast-forward methods, which typically focus on accelerating simulations by identifying stable regions in text game dynamics. Instead, our approach centers on the observation that action sequences in text games often exhibit considerable variability before reaching a stable state, and thus it prioritizes accelerating the most inherently unpredictable aspects of these games. Our results demonstrate that TextWorldExpress accelerates simulations of action effects by 16.8 times, action sequence lengths by 26.4 times, and computation time by 24.8 times, all without a notable decrease in testing accuracy. Moreover, TextWorldExpress is a computationally lightweight framework that can be used in conjunction with various fast-forward strategies and different text game simulation environments. Our framework and associated data are available for public use at https://github.com/Yangzw123 TextWorldExpress. Our findings also reveal that the efficacy of TextWorldExpress is robust and universally applicable across diverse text game benchmarks, including the intensive 30-room TextWorld benchmark, which involves evaluating policy generalization in complex environments. Our research demonstrates that TextWorldExpress can be a valuable tool for the text-based game community by enabling the large-scale testing required for developing more stable and predictable text games. To address growing concerns about the reliability of electricity supplies, electricity systems are increasingly subject to strict standards and quality controls. As a result, the need to manage variations in power production and consumption through redispatch services has increased. Despite this need, implementing redispatch services poses challenges, particularly in designing suitable mechanisms that balance costs and fairness. We examine an all-or-none design for redispatch services where the grid operator can purchase services from specific producers, but not from others. Our analysis shows that this design allows the grid operator to manage power imbalances more effectively, but also creates incentives for producers to misreport their energy production capabilities. To address this issue, we propose a method where the grid operator can prevent producer fraud by limiting the number of orders it places, but this restriction can drive up costs. To mitigate this effect, we suggest introducing a minimum order threshold, which we prove can reduce costs without increasing costs for other producers. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of this design in laboratory settings with human subjects, showing that it can reduce costs compared to traditional methods, but only if the grid operator has sufficient flexibility to cancel orders. We also find that the minimum order threshold helps reduce costs in cases where the grid operator has limited cancellation power. Finally, we analyze the robustness of our results to various parameters, including the number of subjects, the size of the laboratory network, and the minimum order threshold. We also compare our results with existing all-or-none designs in laboratory settings, finding that our design yields higher costs in some cases, but is more efficient in others. We further examine the robustness of our results to various real-world scenarios, including with random producer preferences, and find that our design remains efficient in these cases. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for current redispatch design frameworks used in practice, highlighting potential limitations and areas for future research. In this paper, we establish a polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, which involves counting the number of polynomials with distinct roots from a given field, and specifically zero or one coefficients that contribute to a particular root. Our result includes an explicit count of the contributing polynomials with coefficients in the finite field $F_p$ for a prime number $p$, yielding a result that is expressed as a sum of terms involving $p$-adic integers and is further investigated under the assumption of the Riemann hypothesis. By examining the distribution of these terms, we determine the subset of prime numbers less than $p^n$ that correspond to polynomials with a specific root structure over the field with $p^n$ elements, and this result is tied to the Galois groups of a certain class of global function fields. Ultimately, our findings provide a connection between the count of contributing polynomials and the irreducible representations of the Galois group of the function fields. We also identify patterns in this representation, which include a significant subset consisting of a family of finite fields with Gl_2, Heisenberg, and trivial representations, among others. Moreover, our study reveals that the representation corresponding to a particular subset of prime numbers, including those greater than 3, is equivalent to the character of the Galois group of the function fields over a base field with a specific property. This base field is then characterized and demonstrated to correspond to a class of global function fields with a specific embedding edge (Δ) that is distinct from those with (Δ') or (Δ'') types. Furthermore, our results also encompass the investigation of prime numbers represented by quadratic residues or non-residues, which is tied to the study of a particular Galois group with a mass distribution that is Tetracenic in nature. This Tetracenic distribution was initially observed in the works of Conway and Guy, among others, and our study demonstrates that this distribution arises from the Tetracenic structure of the Galois group rather than the coefficient distribution per se. We further explore the connection between this Tetracenic distribution and the associated polynomial properties. Our research methodology involves an inductive approach that begins with an examination of small fields, which serve as base cases, and then considers large fields through the use of an inductive hypothesis tied to the Galois groups rather than the fields themselves. This paper presents a detailed examination of Saturn's North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), which is contrasted intriguingly with the observed south polar features during Saturn's summer. Despite expectations of a seasonal shift in the north due to Saturn's 26.5-year axial precession, the NPSV retains its distinctive structure. By utilizing data from the Cassini-Huygens space telescope, particularly infrared spectra from the VLT CASSIS instrument and images from the Cassini imaging camera, researchers studied the NPSV's composition, cloud patterns, and temperature patterns. The findings indicate that the north polar vortex maintains its independence, with little interference from the massive anticyclonic flow that normally influences the stratosphere during Saturn's northern summer. The absence of this typical seasonal phenomenon can be attributed to the exceptional robustness of the NPSV. The paper further reveals that the vortex's cloud layers exhibit minimal vertical migration, a distinguishing feature from the massive storm pattern observed in the equatorial region, and the polar vortex's circular shape is maintained through a unique balance of pressure gradients and the presence of a global atmospheric wave double jet structure. The exceptional resilience of the NPSV is highlighted by its minimal impact from the massive storm pattern in the equatorial region, which occurs during the northern summer, and the consequent formation of a persistent anticyclonic flow that shapes the global atmospheric dynamics of Saturn. The research on the NPSV also uncovered a previously unknown polar stratospheric cold layer at mid-latitudes, which displays a notable temperature gradient of 3.5 K per kilometer and may contribute to the vortex's robustness by reducing the upward migration of atmospheric waves. The discovery of this polar stratospheric cold layer was made possible by the high spatial and temporal data resolution provided by the Cassini-Huygens space telescope, which allowed for a detailed analysis of the Saturnian atmosphere through the formation of a global map with a resolution of 0.1 degrees latitude/longitude. This research on the NPSV and the associated polar stratospheric cold layer was made possible by the high spatial and temporal data resolution provided by the Cassini-Huygens space telescope, which enabled the creation of a high-resolution global map of the Saturnian atmosphere. This research integrates Lie algebras and Lie groups, incorporating elements from differential geometry to analyze the measure of orbits. We develop a precise image measure on each orbit, mirroring the original measure on the Lie algebra, and prove this measure is invariant under the action of the group. To demonstrate the invariance, we break down the process into several steps, such as establishing a connection between Kirillov's measure and the geometric measure on orbits, analyzing the relationship between the measure on co-adjoint orbits and the action of the group, and using this relationship to define the measure on the space of admissible pairs, which represents the set of pairs consisting of the Lie algebra and its adjoint action. Finally, we demonstrate that this measure satisfies certain properties, specifically showing that it induces a measure on which the group acts trivially, demonstrating that this measure is invariant under the action of the group. Furthermore, we discover additional measures satisfying these properties, comparing them to the original measure, and analyzing their relationship. This research is an expansion of previous work on Lie algebras and Lie groups, building upon the foundation established in 'The Relationship between the Measure of Adjoint Orbits and the Action of the Group'. It has been submitted to the journal 'Lie Groups and Its Applications'. It has been accepted for publication after revisions guided by referee feedback. The growing complexity of x-ray scattering experiments stems in part from increasing energy ranges and the need to analyze comprehensive data sets. As a result, existing phase retrieval methods may fail to accurately reconstruct the underlying energy spectrum from x-ray Compton scattering data, particularly at synchrotron facilities where high-energy ranges are common. To address this challenge, a novel algorithm has been developed to enhance the precision of energy spectrum reconstruction beyond the capabilities of current methods. This new approach leverages a meta-learning framework, incorporating multiple initial guesses of energy spectra to guide the retrieval of Compton scattering cross-sections, and has been successfully tested on simulated data featuring complex molecular samples, including organic liquids and biological proteins. By evaluating the performance of both traditional and novel methods using mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), the research demonstrates substantial improvements in energy spectrum recovery, with reductions in MAPE of 34.6% for liquid water and 51.8% for bovine serum albumin. Furthermore, the developed algorithm exhibits robust performance across various initial conditions, making it a valuable tool for recovering spectrum information from x-ray Compton scattering data in energy ranges supported by synchrotron facilities. The resulting code has been made publicly available to facilitate the wide adoption of x-ray scattering experiments across multiple energy spectra. The novel algorithm and accompanying benchmarks can be found in the following repository: https://github.com/xinghehu/phaseretrival_metadata. Our analysis focuses on GAs without a fitness function, where solutions interact and the Hamming distance between them determines the payoff. Our primary observation is the existence of a Nash Equilibrium (NE) that varies greatly between these two learning environments. In the ne, the Hamming distance between solutions is consistently lower than the average observed in the corresponding non-coevolutionary scenarios. Our key findings reveal the following differences in ne dynamics: (a) the associated Hamming distance is uniform rather than random, (b) the associated Hamming distance differs from the distances found in searches within non-coevolutionary scenarios, (c) the NE remains stable across changes in population size, (d) the NE remains stable across changes in mutation rate, and (d) the NE remains stable across changes in problem difficulty. Our research confirms the presence of NE dynamics in GAs without a fitness function and highlights the distinct characteristics of ne learning in both individual and social settings. Our results also indicate that ne learning in both settings can be characterized as 'trapped in an optimal local minimum'. Our research further reveals the differences in ne dynamics between individual and social learning, showing that ne associated Hamming distances are higher in social than individual learning settings in both random and fixed topologies. Neural networks are susceptible to subtle errors caused by hardware malfunctions, leading to compromised performance and safety. Existing methods primarily focus on reducing precision, which prioritizes efficiency over accuracy in the presence of errors. In contrast, our approach ensures the integrity of neural networks by limiting input ranges, taking a different path to enhance resilience. We demonstrate that non-uniform range restriction techniques, combined with weight normalization, provide significant protection against performance degradation resulting from errors and is efficient when compared to other robustification techniques. Our approach shows substantial improvements in maintaining performance in the presence of errors for multiple neural network applications, including real-world implementations using real-world data. Moreover, our approach generates minimal overhead during training, making it a promising solution for the robustness of neural networks against faults. J/ψ and D^0 particles were identified through their decay into two muons, while J/ψ particles were also identified directly.  J/ψ and D^0 particles were found to exhibit similar multiplication patterns in small-scale proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus collisions, differing from J/ψ in medium-sized nucleus-nucleus collisions. This approach, which utilizes Brzozowski's operator and a value judgment function, serves as a basis for an efficient algorithm for checking the containment of regular expressions with time and space complexities of O(n+m) each, where n and m represent the number of steps to evaluate the first expression against a given input and the number of steps to evaluate the second expression against that same input respectively. Given regular expressions of sizes p and q, the space and time requirements also are O(pq), where pq represents the number of transitions in the abstract machine used to compare the two expressions. This decision procedure includes a symbolic algorithm for checking containment of regular languages with negative closures, as well as a more efficient algorithm for checking containment of negative closures without the need for symbolic manipulation. These algorithms build upon the work of Emmesberger and Ruskey and provide a more efficient solution to the problem of checking containment of regular expressions with negated conjunctions. This research was inspired by the problem of verifying regular expression-based properties of finite state machines. This approach is particularly effective for checking the consistency of two regular expressions that are related to each other, such as the regular expression describing an language and the mirror image of that language. This decision procedure can be applied to a broader class of expressions known as regular expression fragments, which include many popular variants of regular expressions. These variants include conventional regular expressions with the star operator, anti-congruence regular expressions, and mirror-invariant regular expressions. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of Brzozowski's operator-based decision procedures for a range of problems, including verifying the containment of regular expressions with negated conjunctions, checking the consistency of two mutually exclusive regular expressions, as well as verifying the equivalence and containment of regular expression fragments. This approach is highly efficient, requiring only a linear amount of time and space, making it suitable for large-scale applications. To compare the results, standard and non-standard oxidation processes were tested and carrier concentration profiles obtained from the etched silicon were simulated using the measured oxide layer thickness and carrier concentration in the buffer oxide.  The simulation showed that when looking at the interface between the oxide and silicon, carrier concentration in etched silicon is higher than in the buffer oxide, however the difference diminishes further from the interface.  Additionally, high-density plasma etching was tested and it was found to be less effective than wet etching methods for modifying the carrier concentration in silicon.  Furthermore, the study found that the carrier concentration in etched silicon varies significantly along the width of a sample, more so than along the length, suggesting it may be a critical factor to consider in the design of future silicon photonics components that use etching to create carrier concentration gradients. Despite the name suggestion implying a direct connection to nonlinear Hawkes processes, the proposed model, unlike its counterpart, facilitates estimation and inference techniques. A nonlinear Hawkes process is defined by a system of integral equations, and we establish the existence of solutions given certain conditions. Furthermore, we derive the network architecture from the inverse problem of estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters. Additionally, we outline an algorithm for estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters using the EM algorithm. Simulation experiments demonstrate that nonlinear Hawkes processes can replicate observed interaction patterns and that the proposed model accurately estimates process parameters. Notably, nonlinear Hawkes processes provide a framework for modeling the complex interactions observed in the Wikipedia revision process. This research provides a foundation for further development of nonlinear Hawkes processes, including extensions to handle missing data and model selection. Finally, we discuss possible extensions to the model and associated methods, including nonlinear Hawkes processes with temporal evolution, nonlinear Hawkes processes with network structures derived from observed data, and point process models that combine nonlinear Hawkes processes and exponential random graph models. This research has implications for the analysis of security incidents, Internet traffic patterns, and financial transactions, among other applications. This approach can also be applied to any time-stamped and typed dataset comprising interactions. Prior analysis revealed its unusual chemical element abundance pattern,
with nickel and iron levels relative to each other being exceptionally low.
When compared to the standard supernova abundance ratios, the findings
were so distinct that some researchers suggested it might be explained by
a double supernova event.
However, a new study suggests an alternative theory: a superdense neutron star
with a strong magnetic field collapsed to form the supernova SN~2020jfo.
The research shows that a neutron star with a magnetic field like the one
inferred from the X-ray data can explain the observed nickel and iron levels. 
Additionally, this new perspective also explains the absence of helium

The predicted properties of the supernova SN~2020jfo's central object also

We present a novel approach to interpreting cross-like images formed by lobster-eye optics, leveraging the azimuthal rotation angle to dissect the image and a adjacent mirrorized duplicate. This allows for the identification of distinct parts of the optics system and enables the precise localization of objects within its field of view. By analyzing the intersection points of the radial and azimuthal patterns in the image, we can determine the 4-fold symmetry features such as crossbones, square patterns, or spaced bars and ankles. Furthermore, by interpreting the differences in the duplicate image, we can determine the orientation of these features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using simulations of a 600 nm wavelength X-ray full-range spectrum imaging system. This approach provides a versatile technique for interpreting complex images formed by lobster-eye optics in various applications. Nonetheless, this method might face limitations when dealing with superimposed targets or noise-intensive data. Nonetheless, this research opens up possibilities for extending lobster-eye optics to identify targets with acute symmetry, even in the presence of partial mirrors. To that end, we propose an enhanced design featuring a rotation stage for the detector, which enables the azimuthal analysis of the formed images. This leads to a proposal for a novel metric, the symmetry transfer function, that characterizes the performance of such an optics system. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the wide-ranging capabilities of lobster-eye optics, from wide-spectrum imaging to target identification, based on the interpretation of a single cross-like image. Nonetheless, the true potential of this technology remains unchanged and relies on the assumption that the azimuthal rotation angle does not significantly impact the modulation transfer function of the optics system. Consequently, we propose testing this assumption through rotation-based measurements of the point spread function of lobster-eye optics in the X-ray spectrum. A key factor influencing this task is the accuracy of density fluctuations beyond simply using two-density-field models. Our research used cosmological simulations with a specific amplitude of initial scalar perturbations to compare the halo mass prediction accuracy of different density models, particularly focusing on the effectiveness of two-density-field models compared to three-density-field models, and mapping techniques. A significant discrepancy in halo masses was observed when using a two-density-field model, particularly in over-predicting masses for denser regions and under-predicting masses for less dense regions. This discrepancy was particularly pronounced in areas with $1.5 \rho_c < \rho < 100 \rho_c$, and the scatter was too large, resulting in a halo mass function that combines the original distribution with a logarithmic width of 0.8. In contrast, three-density-field models or mapping techniques yielded only a minor adjustment in the halo mass function, specifically a width of 0.2. Nonetheless, the more significant challenge is related to the underlying physics rather than the model itself, as observed when changing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations from 1 to 3.5, and reducing the observed effect of using a density-only model on halo mass prediction accuracy in these simulations. A novel approach is employed to investigate the evolution of rotating stars by introducing a probability distribution to account for mass, angular momentum, and other properties among fluid elements. This method, which assigns property weights to fluid elements, offers a contrasting perspective to the usual practice of treating each element with specific properties. To accommodate this change of perspective, a statistical formulation is developed and a combination of weight elimination processes identified. A Nordström model is used to apply and validate this approach, revealing the emergence of a probability distribution that reflects the irregular distribution of angular momentum and mass within the star. By comparing the approach to traditional methods, differences in the evolution of stars are observed, most noticeably in the mass-loss phase where the weight approach shows the occurrence of a neutron star formation. This study reveals that the assignment of property weights significantly influences the outcomes of star evolution simulations, thereby highlighting the value of this novel approach. The resulting code for the Nordström model is presented, and the relevant research data made available for download. The code and data can be utilized to explore other models and research questions, and are particularly relevant to the study of rotating neutron stars. The research presented in this study is a preliminary step towards applying this novel approach to models involving neutron stars, and has implications for the assignment of property weights among fluid elements in general. A common and resource-intensive challenge in learning models is gathering labeled data. This issue can be mitigated through selective labeling, an optimizing process that identifies the most informative data among existing unlabelled sources and targets for labeling. This process is particularly valuable in large-scale learning applications. Currently, determining the most informative data relies on heuristic approaches that evaluate data based on features and probabilities, but these methods are often inefficient and unsuitable for real-world settings due to their high computational costs and limitations of existing algorithms. In response to these limitations, this study presents a groundbreaking framework for efficient selective labeling, thereby enabling the acquisition of labeled data for a wide range of tasks and reducing overall costs. This framework's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted across multiple datasets and scenarios, showing that it achieves data evaluations that are both accurate and computationally affordable, thus providing a scalable solution for real-world applications. This approach has been made open-source and is available on GitHub. Furthermore, to facilitate practical implementation, this study also outlines a scalable architecture for embedding the model in real-world settings, thereby enabling the integration of newly labeled data into existing machine learning models through techniques such as incremental learning. This research has far-reaching implications for various machine learning applications, including but not limited to, the enhancement of natural language processing, reinforcement learning, and deep learning, among others. This study has been published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. This research explores the consequences of the pandemic on diversity of urban encounters in three major US cities. Due to lockdown measures, mobility restrictions, and fear of contagion, people's opportunities for running into others in public spaces were significantly curtailed. As a result, urban residents encountered fewer diverse strangers than before. To recover from this decline, cities will need to invest in public spaces that foster community resilience in the face of future epidemics. To achieve this, we propose developing an index to gauge diversity of urban encounters. This index could serve as a vital tool for policymakers and urban planners seeking to maintain the vibrancy of public spaces. By incorporating diversity of urban encounters into their framework, they can ensure that community resilience is given equal priority to other aspects of public health in those spaces. Furthermore, this index can be utilized to monitor the impact of future public health crises on urban diversity and identify effective strategies for recovery. Failing to address this issue may result in permanent loss of diversity in urban encounters, exacerbating social segregation in cities. To illustrate the application of this proposed index, we present a hypothetical example of how it could be used in the context of a future pandemic scenario. By doing so, we highlight the value of this proposed measure in a scenario that, unfortunately, remains all too possible. Meanwhile, the pandemic has already significantly shaped urban encounters in the present time, awaiting necessary policy responses from urban authorities. By leveraging qualitative data from interviews with urban residents, as well as quantitative information from mobility patterns, our analysis reveals the substantial impact the pandemic has had on diversity of urban encounters in these cities. Consequently, their public spaces are in need of enhanced community engagement to regain their pre-pandemic vitality. By reviewing existing literature on diversity of urban encounters, we found that encounters with diverse strangers in public spaces are crucial for promoting community resilience, whereas lockdown measures and reduced mobility have significantly curtailed such opportunities. Given the limited scope of this research, further, larger-scale studies are necessary to thoroughly examine the effect of the pandemic on diversity of urban encounters in the face of community resilience in cities across the world. Nonetheless, as a preliminary examination, this research remains significant due to its unique focus on the three major US cities mentioned earlier, thereby contributing original data and analysis on the intangible aspect of public spaces that, unlike physical infrastructure, has not been monitored for changes during the pandemic. Given the significant impact of the pandemic on urban encounters in these cities, the need for policy interventions to safeguard community resilience in public spaces against future crises is evident. Around a young, massive star with a gravitational influence, objects such as planets, or planetesimals can migrate through a dissipating disc. Mathematical models suggest that this migration could exacerbate instability in the inner disc, leading to the formation of narrow, dense accretion discs, or'mini-discs'. To better understand these'mini-discs' and their possible flavours, we used computational simulations to model the inner 0.04 AU of a star with 12 solar masses for the past few years, incorporating migrating objects that accumulate in the outer part of the star's gravitational reach, and'mini-discs' forming and breaking apart. As time passed, the formation of'mini-discs' slowed due to migrating objects absorbing excess energy and gaining enough momentum to escape the star's gravitational influence. Another phenomenon emerged in the later stages: objects migrating directly towards the star, with sufficient speed to overcome its gravitational force, could reach the innermost regions, contributing to a permanent, stable disc around the massive star. This phenomenon could influence the distribution of objects in the disc, and ultimately, the star itself, shaping its final stages over millions of years. Our simulations also examined the effects of objects migrating in the disc on its dynamics, revealing oscillations in the star and a circularisation process of the orbit, as well as the formation of a stable disc leading to slower mass loss from the massive star, and the possible formation of a binary star system. Our results demonstrate how migrating objects in a massive star's disc can alter its dynamics, leading to the destruction of'mini-discs', yet also creating a permanent, stable disc around the massive star, which can influence the massive star's evolution over millions of years. Our simulations provide the first detailed investigation of migrating objects in a massive star's disc, offering insights into the distribution of objects, the formation of'mini-discs', and the binary star formation, as well as the physical processes at work, including gravitational interactions, accretion, and gravitational runoff bars. Our computational tool can be applied to model migrating planets in lower mass star systems. This research develops a novel method to transform the conventional stream function formulation of water wave problems, enabling the reconstruction of surface elevation from the envelope of waves. Originally proposed by Longuet-Higginbottom, this approach uses a stream function to describe the underlying flow, but we've modified it to accommodate the new perspective on wave geometry. In the standard approach, the stream function leads to the conservation of vorticity, but we've introduced a modification causing a buildup of vorticity, which we refer to as 'effective vorticity'. By substituting the original conservation equation with one that includes effective vorticity, we've created a second evolution equation that can be used in conjunction with the original equation to form a nonlinear system of Hamiltonian form. This system provides the necessary information to construct the wave envelope and surface elevation reconstruction, and it has been proven to be a well-posed problem. Additionally, we've established that our modification preserves the uniform bound of the solution, which is crucial for demonstrating the global existence and infinite-time asymptotic stability of the solution. Furthermore, we've successfully applied this new approach to solve the initial value problem for both infinite and finite water depth cases. Moreover, our research has been extended to investigate the behavior of waves in a domain with a finite barrier at one end, which we've termed the 'wave driver problem'. In this variant, we've established the existence and uniqueness of the solution, as well as its infinite-time asymptotic stability. It is noteworthy that our 'effective vorticity' approach can be viewed as an alternative perspective on the well-known Birkhoff normal form equation by pushing it further to recover the original form of the conservation equation. It is also notable that our research was conceived during the author's tenure at the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute. It is also worth mentioning that the term 'water wave problems' refers to a set of nonlinear partial differential equations that describe wave behavior in fluid surfaces guided by the force of gravity, and it is denoted by the BBM equation and the Camassa-Holm equation among others. It is also necessary to mention that our research was motivated by the author's previous research on the Camassa-Holm equation. This paper delves into the fundamentals of differential forms within locally convex spaces, and it significantly expands upon the surface layer theorem to provide a useful tool for analysis. By transforming the surface layer theorem into an equivalent statement, we gain insight into the properties of differential forms and their gradients. Furthermore, we prove that the space of differential forms integrates the characteristics of Taylor series expansion spaces, thereby establishing a connection to the framework of analytic functions. Moreover, we establish that the differential forms satisfy the properties of Cauchy-Riemann operators within locally convex spaces. Finally, we introduce the concept of harmonic functions in the context of locally convex spaces and prove that they satisfy the surface layer theorem. This enables us to define analytic functions and investigate their properties, including convergence and series expansion. Moreover, we establish that the Laplace operator can be accurately represented by means of a generator, which facilitates the discussion of analytic and harmonic functions. This representation also leads to an examination of the operator's invertibility and its connection to the space of harmonic functions. By further expanding upon this relationship, we discover additional properties related to the operator's spectrum and its connection to the spaces of analytic and harmonic functions. This research builds upon the work presented in the book by H. Gluher, titled "Differential Forms and Taylor Series Expansion Spaces", which served as a primary source of knowledge for the current study. In addition, the surface layer theorem in this paper has been extensively generalized to accommodate not only Euclidean spaces but also other types of metric spaces, thereby broadening its applicability. This paper introduces a novel navigation control system for a mobile robot at sea, which employs a layered control structure to efficiently navigate the sea floor. The layered control system amplifies the robot's navigation capabilities by combining a local trajectory controller and a controller that navigates the sea floor. The sea floor navigation controller guarantees the robot's ability to traverse the sea floor seamlessly by controlling its position and orientation. To implement this controller, we develop a method to determine the sea floor coordinates from sonar sensor data, which involves establishing a registration system to link sensor readings to floor coordinates and calculating the floor coordinates from beam data. This approach enables the robot to build a map of the sea floor around it by integrating new sonar data to the existing map. Furthermore, we devise a method to estimate the robot's orientation from sonar beam data using a nonlinear filter, which facilitates the navigation of the robot through narrow passages. To evaluate the robot's navigation capabilities, we conducted simulations of navigation through a virtual sea floor mapped with sonar data. These simulations showed that the robot's navigation through the sea floor is robust and predictable. Additionally, we present experimental results of the robot's navigation through the sea floor in a real-world setting. We investigate the interplay of curvature effects, hysteresis, and phase transitions in dynamic systems powered by an external drive and controlled through a variable temperature-like parameter. Our primary focus is on the curvature of a dimensionless energy function, which drives a mobile agent, and we analyze how it influences the agent's trajectory and the resulting phase transitions and hysteresis. To model this situation, we use a simple dynamical system with a van der Waals type curve and investigate the boundary curves separating different phases in the plane defined by the temperature-like parameter and the average curvature. Furthermore, we examine the development of hysteresis and the switching between different phase transitions as the curvature changes over time. The effects of the curvature on the system's entropy and the shape of the boundary curves are also studied as the temperature-like parameter varies. To broaden our understanding, we consider additional scenarios, including a rational function with first-order asymptotes and a sinusoidally varying curvature. Our findings are further illustrated with numerical examples. Finally, we discuss the implications of our study for the dynamics of the mobile agent and the resulting phase transitions in relation to the curvature of its surrounding environment. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through the application of our methodology to well-known models, including the Ising model, the Kuramoto model, and the Lotka-Volterra system. Our research reveals that the hysteresis effect can persist even in the presence of large amplitude oscillations in the temperature-like parameter, thereby indicating that the resulting phase transitions are robust and irreversible. The evaluation of the system's entropy shows that the maximum entropy occurs at a curvature value of zero, both for the van der Waals type curve and the rational function with first-order asymptotes. The robustness of our findings is validated through the implementation of various numerical methods, including the fourth-order Newton-Raphson method, the fifth-order Newton-Raphson method, the shooting method, and the fourth-fifth order combined method. The advantages and limitations of each method are tested in relation to their precision, robustness, and computational efficiency. The results of our study highlight the crucial impact of the curvature effect on the dynamics of mobile agents in non-uniform environments and emphasize the significance of considering curvature when analyzing and controlling dynamic phase transitions and hysteresis. To address the challenging problem of L1-PCA on real symmetric matrices, specifically when the underlying distribution is rotationally symmetric, researchers have proposed various alternatives. Although these alternatives have achieved compelling results, there is still a significant gap in resolving the problem for its most constrained form, which involves minimizing the sum of the absolute values of matrix eigenvalues. To overcome this difficulty, a two-block formulation was introduced, however this variant is sensitive to noise and requires an approximation method. Compared to traditional approaches, neural network-based natural language processing models yield better performance, yet it is crucial to ensure the accuracy of their annotations by detecting inconsistencies. We propose a method to achieve this via semantic labeling tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, where we treat the existing annotations as labeled data and the original annotations as target labels to be predicted. By evaluating the model's performance on a micro-f1 score across these tasks, we find a significant gap between the model's actual performance and its self-perceived ability, indicating numerous inconsistencies in the annotations. To rectify this, we employ paraphrase detection on the tasks' output, resulting in a significant reduction in the number of inconsistencies, from 31% to 11% on average across the tasks examined. Furthermore, our approach outperforms a baseline approach utilizing a plain text classifier on these tasks, which involves identifying inconsistencies in the output generated by the model alone. Our approach also yields an environmentally friendly cost, as the model itself incites many of the necessary annotations required to train the paraphrase detector, thereby minimizing the additional annotation required. Achieving efficient and effective navigation through vast public spaces like airports and shopping centers is crucial, especially with the rising popularity of wearable and mobile navigation devices. These spaces have multiple entrances and exits, differing paths for navigating, and varying distance criteria, all of which traditional mapping systems were designed to address. In response to these challenges, the HiTMap framework was developed, which splits the map into two distinct parts: a simplified graph representing the shortest path, and a detailed two-layer layout for navigation by foot. This navigation method considers two distance standards and accounts for walking paths between locations. In this paper, we have developed HiTMap generation guidelines for airports and shopping centers. We tested these guidelines on real-world examples and conducted a usability assessment among participants. Furthermore, we present algorithms for creating HiTMap representations and offer an interactive demo of the HiTMap viewer. The research, data, and software developed are all openly available for public use.

We investigated the atomic arrangement of carbon and nitrogen in interstitial sites of rutile TiO2 using ab initio calculations. Comparing these results with substituted C and N in Ti sites or O sites revealed significant differences in band structure and electronic properties. Notably, in some cases, C and N in interstitial sites presented semiconductor characteristics, contrary to their metallic behavior when substituted in Ti or O sites. Additionally, we found that N in interstitial sites had a smaller band gap than C, and this gap could be adjusted by applying pressure. These findings suggest that N in interstitial sites may exhibit p-type semiconductor properties and that C or N in these sites could act as charge compensation defects when Ti or O sites are substituted with C or N. Therefore, their coexistence might be crucial for achieving high conductivity in TiO2-based materials. Moreover, we determined the formation energies of C and N in interstitial sites, with results indicating that N is more stable at higher oxygen pressures, while C is more stable at higher pressures, and that they both become more stable with increasing pressure. Moreover, our calculations showed that C or N in interstitial sites form pairs with oxygen vacancies, while pairs with each other require higher formation energies. Lastly, our work includes the discussion of possible experimental verification using synthetic methods that control oxygen pressure.

Subsequently, upper limits on branching ratios are established at 95% confidence levels: one scenario based on assumed massive neutral scalar mediation results in a limit of 1.25 x 10^-4, while another scenario with massive neutral vector mediation results in a limit of 0.46 x 10^-4; alternatively, limits for neutral pseudoscalar and vector mediations are 0.21 x 10^-4 and 0.37 x 10^-4, respectively; finally, limits for charged scalar and vector mediations are 0.15 x 10^-4 and 0.53 x 10^-4. Qubit-based systems, such as quantum computers, rely on precise mass measurements to maintain reliability. In a breakthrough, our research identifies the inherent limits of mass determination accuracy in qubit systems, demonstrating a direct correlation with the Carleman estimate of the quantum system's generator. By establishing this connection, we theoretically determine the minimum amount of noise a qubit system can tolerate while maintaining the effectiveness of specific mass measurement techniques. Furthermore, our findings reveal that qutrit systems possess greater noise tolerance than qubit systems under certain error conditions, potentially making qutrits a more suitable choice for practical applications. Our study focuses on two error channels: amplitude decay and spontaneous photon switching, for both qubit and qutrit systems. Our research outcomes are applicable to various quantum devices, including trapped ions and cavity QED. In the latter case, our analysis demonstrates that cavity QED offers greater flexibility in designing quantum devices that resist decay-induced noise. A statistical analysis of molecular cores in the Perseus region has provided intriguing results, revealing that many cores with significant mass growth are associated with the outflows of massive molecular masses yet are lacking in signs of massive star formation.  In contrast, only the most mass-intensive cores with outflows are found to give rise to massive stars.  We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that the mass growth of cores is largely unaffected by the massive stars that form from them, rather it is the massive stars that form from cores of massive masses.  As a result, only the most mass-intensive cores are expected to produce massive stars and outflows, while the more moderate mass cores would over time release all their mass and outflows, making them undetectable by now.  Consequently, only those cores that are on the cusp of forming massive stars are likely to be observed today. Classical differentiation and integration operations were investigated in relation to positive definite functions with specific symmetries, known as zonal functions. We discovered that these operations result in positive definite zonal functions at locations other than zero, leading us to further examine the concept of positive definite zonal functions in relation to group transformations. This exploration exposes the connection between these functions and the theory of integral operators associated with positive definite functions. Moreover, our investigation reveals that positive definite zonal functions can be classified into two categories: (1) those characterized by the absence of positivity loss following differentiation or integration, and (2) those characterized by the presence of positivity loss after undergoing these operations. We then establish conditions for positive definiteness after applying differentiation and integration, and we demonstrate examples of both the absence and presence of positivity loss in relation to specific groups of transformations. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for the generation of positive definite zonal functions via the action of integral operators associated with continuous time processes. The applicability and usefulness of these findings are illustrated through the generation of viable models for spatial processes. The underlying theory and developed concepts are also applicable to the special case of radial functions. The model incorporates a roughness factor to capture the altered behavior of liquid foams, which can be viewed as a combination of foam and wetting liquid. The roughness factor's effect is primarily evident in two situations. Firstly, when the surface pressure differs significantly from the value when the foam is alone, the factor affects how the pressure changes in time. Secondly, when there is a wetting liquid present, the factor influences how the pressure changes in time and also affects the liquid's distribution between the foam and the surface. The model has been applied to experimentally obtained data showing surface pressure fluctuations at different depths of a Hele-Shaw cell, filled with liquid and covered in liquid foam. The model has been compared with another model consisting of two timescales, which results in the model with two timescales being a special case of the model with the roughness factor. Convolutional neural networks exhibit high performance in various image classification tasks, however, ensemble classifiers can significantly boost their efficacy. In this research, we investigate how hybrid ensemble classifiers consisting of convolutional neural networks and random forest classify magnetic resonance images. We achieved remarkable results with this combination, surpassing traditional methods consisting of sole convolutional neural networks. Our contribution also includes developing a dataset of 5000 cerebral porencephalic lesions, which is publicly available for future research. We constructed this dataset from cerebral lesions present in normal brain MRI scans and employed a multi-class classification model to verify our ensemble classifier's effectiveness. Our findings show that the hybrid model exhibits a higher accuracy rate of 74.46% in classifying small lesions, compared to convolutional neural networks alone which achieved an accuracy rate of 68.45%. This research demonstrates the efficacy of ensemble classifiers consisting of convolutional neural networks and random forest in classifying large lesions, with results that surpass the capability of sole convolutional neural networks in this task. Our methodology provides a viable solution for automatically detecting cerebral porencephalic lesions in brain MRI scans. Our dataset and code are available online at the following links: https://github.com/Thiago Ferrer/Fetal-Damage-Detection and https://github.com/Thiago Ferrer/Ensemble-ConvNet. This research is an extension of our previous study published at the following link: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/piang/PII109119X21005576. We believe that our methodology and dataset contribute significant value to the community working on MRI-based classification tasks, specifically those involving cerebral porencephalic lesions. We advise future researchers to evaluate our methodology on various brain lesion scenarios. We also propose a new ensemble classifier consisting of convolutional neural networks and random forest that classifies MRI scans containing brain lesions, by leveraging spatial information present in random forest and enhancing its efficacy with convolutional neural networks. This new ensemble classifier consists of six layers, which fuse global and local features, exhibit robust performance when trained on small MRI scan datasets, and demonstrate the efficacy of ensemble classifiers consisting of convolutional neural networks and random forest in classification tasks involving MRI scans. A rotating Hele-Shaw cell filled with a viscous fluid is studied theoretically to examine how the stability of various fluid states is affected by membrane tension. The model includes a circular region experiencing net rotation at its center, surrounded by a large, statically filled region with no rotation. The behavior of this system is analyzed across a range of membrane tension levels, from negative to positive, and its stability is determined by comparing the differences in the rotation rate between the inner and outer regions. The results show that negative membrane tension can lead to an unstable state and cause the rotation rate to increase over time, while positive membrane tension leads to a stable state with rotation rates that decrease over time. The effects of membrane tension on stability in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell with no net rotation at its center also vary and are influenced by the distance over which the rotation rate decreases. The findings of this study have been verified through direct numerical simulation and come from an analytical solution derived from the full set of two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with no spherical symmetry. The research focuses on a specific scenario to highlight the importance of considering membrane tension in the study of rotating Hele-Shaw cells, especially in contexts where the rotation rate increases with time. The term "membrane tension" refers to the force causing the distance between the walls of the Hele-Shaw cell to decrease, which can be driven by a pressure gradient or an external force, and it plays a significant role in the stability of rotating Hele-Shaw cells even when the rotation is uniform over a large distance. The study demonstrates the need for a theory that takes into account the effects of membrane tension on rotating Hele-Shaw cells, building on the established knowledge of the stability of rotating fluid layers with membrane tension, which was first discovered through an analogy with supercritical nuclear fission. The research also highlights the similarities and differences between rotating Hele-Shaw cells and rotating fluid layers. The result of negative membrane tension leading to instability in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell with no net rotation at its center was unknown prior to this study. The study of rotating Hele-Shaw cells also provides the foundation for investigating more complex scenarios, including those with multiple rotating regions, varying rotation rates, and rotating regions surrounded by flowing fluids. The effects of membrane tension on the stability of these scenarios remain unexplored. The research offers a theoretical framework for a specific scenario but has implications for the physical phenomena involved and could influence the design of experiments in the field of fluid dynamics. To enhance neural machine translation, a novel attention mechanism called look-ahead attention has been developed to examine the future context beyond the current position. This approach allows the model to consider both the current and future context when translating early words, and has been integrated into a hierarchical translation model. Experiments conducted on two large-scale translation datasets showed improvements in metrics such as BLEU scores. Specifically, looking-ahead to the future 0--1 sentences appeared to be effective, and this strategy has the added benefit of simplifying the attention network, reducing noise and improving interpretability. The code for this project has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ghru/lookahead-attention.

Scientific computing grids are achieving broad acceptance and a diverse range of applications is emerging. However, a one-way approach to grid development may lead to fragmentation. A proposed translational approach suggests that applications and grids should evolve in parallel, with each informing the other through continuous refinement. This approach is illustrated by using a grid to solve nonlinear optimization problems, where the algorithm's algoriithmic insights improve grid performance, and the economic theory underlying an e-commerce interface enhances grid utilization. These findings indicate that a translational approach can lead to more efficient grids and successful deployment of grid technology. Moreover, this approach can help address issues of scalability and fragility in grid technologies by providing a natural means of handling these problems. As a result, researchers and practitioners are encouraged to adopt a one-way, let alone a two-way, translational approach to grid development, which offers numerous benefits with minimal additional costs. In conclusion, this paper urges the grid community to reconsider its relationship with applications, advocating for a more collaborative stance, with potential rewards awaiting those who embrace this change. In the appendix, the source code of the NEST optimizer is presented alongside the grid implementation, offering a tangible example of a translational approach in action. By interpreting Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized examples of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), we have gained insight into their underlying mechanics. This understanding allows us to reframe several key concepts, such as the limitations of CNNs in modeling long-range spatial relationships and the equivalent capabilities of fully connected Neural Networks and GCs with predefined connections. Furthermore, we have discovered that modifying the architecture of CNNs is equivalent to modifying the graph underlying a GC, and we have explored methods to enhance CNNs by incorporating additional edges based on contextual information. We have also developed a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of CNNs in relation to their underlying graph structure, which we have demonstrated to be a necessary condition for learning short-range spatial relationships. Finally, we have applied this knowledge to design a novel Neural Network that leverages a random graph, and we have compared it to existing state-of-the-art approaches on various image classification tasks. We develop a groundbreaking one-pass algorithm to generate a superior coreset for the $k$-means clustering problem. This coreset reduces the problem's size from approximately $n$ to $O(k \cdot d \cdot \lambda^{-2})$ for data sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $\lambda$ represents the desired accuracy. Our approach achieves this significant reduction while maintaining near-optimal clustering results compared to solving the full problem. Notably, this one-pass algorithm surpasses previous methods that required multiple passes through the data to create coresets, and it does so with a lower memory footprint. Additionally, our algorithm improves upon existing results for $k$-means by utilizing data that is available directly, and it includes an improved analysis to create coresets of higher quality than previously achieved. This is evident in the results of experiments conducted with real data sets and various clustering problems. Furthermore, our algorithm can be integrated with other coreset creation methods to enhance existing solutions. We provide a detailed explanation of our one-pass algorithm along with a general approach to enhance existing coresets using additional data. This enhancement is possible because our one-pass algorithm produces high-quality coarrays that can serve as inputs for other clustering methods. We demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of our algorithm by applying it to experimental data sets and comparing it to other coreset creation methods and clustering algorithms of a high degree of accuracy. This includes Gaussian and uniform models, along with real-world data sets like MNIST and VGGFace2. We also offer a comprehensive evaluation of our algorithm in comparison to other coreset creation methods in order to validate its superiority. This comparison includes standard metrics such as coarray size, clustering error, and execution time. Our one-pass algorithm has a broad applicability to a wide range of clustering problems and related tasks due to its highly adaptable nature. This is made possible by the unique properties of the coarrays it produces, which can be utilized as input for other clustering algorithms, other coreset creation methods, and even machine learning models like neural networks. In complex decision-making scenarios, particularly in large-scale grid worlds, our research introduces a novel method to enhance our understanding and improve our performance. By dividing the grid into distinct regions, known as superstates, our approach provides a clear and concise overview of the environment and its inhabitants. From this perspective, we can make more informed decisions about our next course of action. In the specific context of pursuing evaders, our superstate framework facilitates another key advantage: it allows us to accurately determine the evaders' possible locations and, in turn, significantly enhances our chances of successfully catching them. Two key improvements result from using superstates in this scenario: they reduce the number of possible actions to consider and supply the necessary information to accurately calculate the probability of finding the evaders in certain areas. Through comprehensive simulations, our superstate approach has been shown to significantly improve the outcomes of pursuing evaders, whether they are stationary or move freely, and whether the grid world is small or extremely large. Our research demonstrates that considering a grid world as a multi-state environment can greatly simplify the decision-making process and improve the results in various scenarios. Furthermore, our superstate approach offers a versatile solution that can be applied to various related problems, such as navigating through unknown environments and managing resource distribution among group members. Our software is available for download, and our data are accessible through the Cogitatio Hub research platform. Our research provides a significant contribution to the fields of complex decision-making, group dynamics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in relation to grid world scenarios. Our superstate approach has the potential to be further developed and applied in various real-world settings, such as managing traffic flow, optimizing energy consumption, and navigating social networks. When working on multiple tasks using multi-task reinforcement learning, it's common to encounter several challenges, including the transfer of knowledge and skill completion. However, using a single learned dynamics model for prediction can lead to a potential drawback, causing the agent to lose the ability to navigate certain environments due to model bias. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a unique method called multi-dynamics exploration, which allows the agent to learn and manage multiple separate dynamics models for each task, each with its own unique exploration strategy. 

Through MD-exploration, the agent can easily switch between tasks and environments by simply changing the dynamics model and associated exploration strategy. To achieve this, we've developed a specialized controller that can be shared across all dynamics models, ensuring seamless task transfer without losing previously acquired skills. We've also introduced a novel policy and dynamics learning algorithm (PDDLA) to facilitate efficient learning. Our experiments, conducted across multiple environments from the Gym suite and the Multi-Dynamics dataset, demonstrate superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. 

Our findings reveal that learning separate dynamics models for each task and environment significantly enhances the agent's ability to navigate contexts with different physical properties, such as variation in reward functions and environmental stability. To facilitate broad access to our research, we've made the code and dataset for MD-exploration open-source, available on GitHub at https://github.com/HsiaoJenWang/md-exploration. This work has the potential to be used in various applications, including simulation-to-real transfer and learning in uncertain environments. 
To that end, we've introduced a novel metric called the environment similarity ratio (ESR), which provides a quantitative measure of the similarity between simulations and real-world contexts. Our results show that MD-exploration significantly outperforms current benchmarks in simulation-to-real transfer, as demonstrated in our experiments with the CartPole and LunarLander tasks. 
Our research offers valuable insights into the design of future dynamics models, particularly in relation to the impact of model generalizability and the introduction of random processes, such as Gaussian noise. Our findings suggest that the use of Gaussian noise can actually decrease the effectiveness of model generalizability, leading to a negative impact on the transfer learning ability of the agent. 
Our work has significant implications for the development of future dynamics models, particularly in relation to the impact of random processes, such as Gaussian noise, which our experiments reveal can lead to a negative effect on model generalizability and thus the transfer learning ability of the agent. This research extends Hadamard's three circles theorem to a higher dimensional context, where it takes the form of a significant property of monogenic functions. It demonstrates that when a monogenic function is defined on a specific type of convex body in Dirac operator-based spaces, it exhibits a specific averaging behavior. This paper introduces a novel Wasserstein GAN framework, specifically a conditional version, that generates posterior samples with the help of a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN. Called CWGAN, it seeks to approximate the conditional posterior distribution, which is equivalent to the conditional data manifold. This model takes an additional input and produces an artificial sample that has the same high-dimensional structure as real data. A key advantage of CWGAN is its ability to produce synthetic samples with the same statistical properties as real data, without the need for labeling or explicit calculation of probability distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CWGAN by applying it to three image generation tasks: MNIST, FMNIST, and CelebA, achieving results that are on par with current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in generating real-world faces, where it produces results comparable to BigBiGAN. This leads to a significant improvement in generated image quality compared to previous Wasserstein-based GANs, which are known to struggle with high-resolution, real-world data, relying instead on projection noise, we propose an easy-to-implement optimizer called LookAhead, which enhances CWGAN performance across various tasks and data sets. Notably, CWGAN delivers comparable performance to BIGBIGAN, a state-of-the-art bi-directional GAN, on the CelebA data set, while maintaining a substantial reduction in model size. Additionally, it achieves performance on par with conditional GANs on MNIST and FMNIST, despite having a significantly smaller model size. This is made available as code, along with pre-trained models, on https://github.com/stealthyferret/CWGAN. This research focuses on the compatibility of linear subspaces in fractional order systems under time-varying transformations and constant transformations. For a fractional order system with compatible subspaces, we establish the invariance of a linear subspace with respect to time-varying transformations and constant transformations. Additionally, we provide a method to determine the invariance of a linear subspace with constant coefficients, and then extend this approach to variable coefficients by using an equivalent formulation involving constant coefficients. Furthermore, we explore the concept of compatible subspaces in a fractional order system with variable coefficients, both with and without the presence of external inputs. Finally, we establish relationships between the compatible subspaces and the positive invariance of regions in the state and output spaces. Moreover, we establish conditions for the asymptotic stability of the fractional order system with variable coefficients. We also investigate the positive invariance of regions in the state and output spaces and asymptotic stability in this context. This research supplements previous studies on this topic, which primarily focused on constant coefficients. This research demonstrates that the properties of compatible subspaces in fractional order systems with variable coefficients can be interpreted through the lens of sum-of-powers stability, and provides an extensive bibliography on the related literature and previous results. This research also presents an approach to addressing stability and inertia problems in variable coefficient systems by utilizing the concepts of compatible subspaces and sum-of-powers stability. This approach is then applied to the evaluation of the asymptotic stability of the Rigid Body Mode in a variable coefficient spacecraft. This research was motivated by the experience gained from the development of robust controllers for a variable coefficient Mars Lander, where the need to re-examine the asymptotic stability of the Rigid Body Mode arose during the testing stage. This experience underscored the significance of thoroughly examining the asymptotic stability of variable coefficient systems, particularly in the robust control domain. We introduce a method to compute the topological Hochschild homology of a bicategorical functor from the bicategory of algebras and bimodules to topological spaces. This involves incorporating the concept of shadows, which extends conventional approach to action on bimodules. A specific case leads to an interpretation of the resulting THHH as acting on the suspension of bimodules, effectively giving a functor from the bicategorical THHH to the original domain of the original functor. We apply this framework to calculate the topological cyclic homology of exponential functors, obtaining a simplified structure that includes the descent along subgroups of the underlying ring's automorphism group. Furthermore, we discover that TC involves the total descent along the lower central series of the underlying ring, which it shares with a related construct known as the Taylor series of a ring. The resulting TC also exhibits properties of polynomial rings and exhibits modular properties. Additionally, we establish a connection between the Taylor series and the combinatorial lower central series formula. Moreover, we discover distinct rings whose lower central series formulas are related to particular polynomial rings, which in turn are associated with non-trivial TC constructs. These constructs demonstrate distinct properties, such as the existence of a linear segment with integer length within the set of irreducible components of the associated variety of modules. This segment has a specific length determined by the number of levels in the lower central series, thereby proving a conjecture initially proposed by J. J. Rotman in 1983. We conclude by exploring an illustrative application of this framework to a notable example of a ring, namely, the ring known as G(R,N) constructed from a group R and an integer N. This example reveals that the associated TC exhibits a distinct property marked by a sudden shift in the number of irreducible components of the variety of modules, occurring at the (N-1)th level of the lower central series. This phenomenon remains unobserved in conventional approaches to algebraic geometry. We propose that this unexpected behavior is a result of the incorporation of the shadow component in the Bismuth framework, which provides a meaningful extension of conventional algebraic geometry but also reveals its own distinct limitations and advantages. We emphasize that this notable example, revealing a surprising pattern of modular property with a specific length, can be studied within the conventional algebraic geometry framework only by utilizing an essentially different method. We emphasize that our initial motivation to investigate this particular example of the ring G(R,N) arose from a question initially proposed by H. Miller

Researchers have made significant progress in sound source identification using deep learning, but the lack of a comprehensive dataset has limited progress in this area. To address this challenge, a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) has been created, comprising over 10,000 video clips with clear labels, identifying the primary sound sources within each clip. Unlike existing datasets, VGG-SS encompasses a broad spectrum of sound sources and is dedicated entirely to source identification, without any overlap with existing datasets. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this new dataset, a thorough analysis was conducted involving multiple evaluation methods and benchmarks. A fundamental concept in condensed matter theory, effectively averaging out atomic degrees of freedom to obtain an average or effective behavior, has been used to develop various materials theories. A broad class of transition metal oxides with complex electronic structures can be well explained using this approach, considering the interaction between metal cations and oxygen anions, as well as the spin-orbit coupling of the metal cations. However, the relationship between the effective spin-orbit coupling, the interaction between the atoms, the oxygen anions, and the metal cations, as well as the energy differences (crystal field splitting) between different electronic levels, is generally complex and has not been well understood, especially when strong interactions are present. In this study, we developed a simple average action approach that effectively averages out the degrees of freedom of oxygen anions, obtaining a one-dimensional model that includes spin-orbit coupling and crystal field splitting, and incorporating interaction effects. This research expands on existing theories by combining relative $I$-functions and relative $J$-functions to obtain relative $K$-functions, enabling the creation of explicit mathematical formulas for relative $I$-functions for these varieties and contributing to an in-depth analysis of their geometric properties. Furthermore, this research discovers distinct relationships between the relative $I$-functions of specific varieties with shared components, providing a framework for applying these findings to related topics. This research also develops the concept of relative $J$-functions for these varieties, which are then utilized to establish connections between relative $I$-functions and their underlying geometric structures, thereby establishing the efficacy of this approach for an expanded range of varieties. This expanded framework is then applied to establish a significant connection between the relative $I$-functions and the coefficients of the differential equations that define these varieties, as well as the properties of their component curves. This research is also accompanied by a comprehensive bibliography of published and unpublished works on relative $I$-function theory. This research has significant implications for the study of relative $I$-function theory and its applications in complex geometry and number theory. This study explores the potential of generative models to create new, pathologic anatomical structures by manipulating the underlying representations, with a focus on lung CT images. We propose an innovative approach that leverages the capability of latent code manipulation in these models, enhancing the accuracy of their representations through a training process that mimics human expertise. This process, which we call "pathological knowledge distillation," transfers knowledge from more experienced models by guiding them along a path that reflects both regional anatomy and common abnormalities, as listed in the Radiology-BERT knowledge graph. Our results show that this approach improves the fidelity of generated representations when evaluated using the MediQA benchmark, which assesses the ability of models to answer medical questions based on their representations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach enhances the ability of these models to detect anomalies in lung CT images, achieving the best anomaly detection rate among the compared methods, including popular techniques like deep domain confusion and adversarial learning. This approach has the advantage of being universally applicable to any generative model and lung CT analysis task, making it a significant contribution to the field. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghali97/LATENT-LUNG-CT-ANOMALY-Detection.
